sens: A Roman unit of distance equal to a thousand paces
Approximately 1480 meters, slightly less than our kilometer
A journey that one travels on foot
G3400.detail:
1. The word refers to a Roman measure of length: a thousand paces, which the Romans called milliarium. It is a precise, standardized distance used to measure roads. This unit was well known in the Greco-Roman world of the first century.

2. Specifically, a mile represents approximately 1480 meters — a little less than our current kilometer. It is a distance that can be walked in about twenty minutes at a normal pace.

3. In everyday life, a mile is simply a path to take, a distance that separates two points. In Matthew 5:41, Jesus speaks of someone who "forces you to go one mile": it is the image of a chore, an obligation imposed on a traveler.
G3400.origine: The Greek word milion comes directly from the Latin mille, which means "thousand" (the number). A Roman mile was worth a thousand double paces (mille passus). The Romans marked roads with milestone markers, hence the name. The word is borrowed from Roman military and administrative vocabulary, as it was Rome that instituted this system of measurement.
G3400.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 5:41. Jesus uses it in his teaching on loving enemies and self-giving: he speaks of a man forced by an authority (probably Roman) to carry a soldier's burden for a mile. This was a historical reality in Jesus' time — the Romans had the right to impose this chore on local inhabitants. Jesus takes this concrete and popular term to teach forgiveness and generosity beyond constraint.
G3400.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on Jesus' words regarding generosity without calculation. When one is forced to do something, doing more becomes an act of freedom and love. The mile is not just a distance: it is the image of self-transcendence, a richness of heart that gives more than what is asked of us.

sens: To reproduce the behavior or example of someone
To take the actions or way of life of another as a model
To voluntarily adopt the way of acting of another
To conform to the practices of those we admire or recognize as authority
G3401.detail:
1. The word to imitate primarily means to reproduce or copy the way of acting of someone else — not by constraint, but by deliberately choosing to do as they do. When Paul says to the Thessalonians, "You know how you ought to imitate us" (2 Thessalonians 3:7), he speaks of following his example of diligent and orderly living.
2. It also means to take someone as a model because of qualities we admire or that they represent. The author of Hebrews exhorts his readers to "imitate the faith" of their leaders (Hebrews 13:7) — not to mechanically copy their actions, but to follow the same path of trust in God that they have shown.
3. In practice, to imitate involves a positive intention: one consciously chooses to conform to what is good. That is why John writes, "Do not imitate evil, but good" (3 John 1:11) — imitation can follow both evil and good, but the disciple must orient their choice toward good.
4. Finally, it is an act of recognition toward those we acknowledge as spiritual guides or authorities: to imitate is to honor and follow those in whom we see wisdom, righteousness, or faith.
G3401.origine: The word comes from the Greek mimος (mimos), which designated an actor or imitator in theater — one who reproduced or played the actions of others. From there, the verb to imitate was born, which retains this idea of reproduction, but applied to real life and not theater. The root expresses the action of visually following someone's model and reproducing it.
G3401.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, always to exhort believers to follow a positive example. Paul uses it in his two letters to the Thessalonians (3:7 and 3:9) to invite his disciples to imitate his modest and diligent way of life; he sees it as an effective pedagogical means of transmitting lived faith, not just taught by word. The epistle to the Hebrews (13:7) applies the term to the faith of the former leaders: to imitate here means to reproduce their spiritual attitude before God. Finally, John adds a moral dimension: to imitate is to choose between good and evil (3 John 1:11). In all cases, the word never denotes a mechanical mimicry, but the voluntary adoption of a worthy lifestyle.
G3401.portee: For the Christian, imitation is not a mere child's play: it is a biblical path of learning and spiritual growth. The New Testament invites us to imitate the living examples of faith and righteousness that God places on our path — pastors, apostles, elders — and to cultivate discernment between what deserves to be imitated (the good, faith, righteousness) and what must be rejected (evil). It is also recognizing that faith is transmitted first by lived example, not just by words.

sens: one who reproduces or imitates the behavior of another person
one who follows the model and example of a master or authority
one who adopts the convictions and lifestyle of another
G3402.detail:
1. In its primary and concrete sense, an imitator is someone who reproduces what they see done by another person. It is an act of copying, of mimicry: one observes, sees, and does the same thing. It is simple and direct.

2. In the Bible, this word always designates one who takes a worthy model and voluntarily imitates it, out of admiration and attachment. Paul asks the Corinthians, "Be imitators of me" (1 Corinthians 4:16), not out of vanity, but because he offers the example of Christ. Imitation becomes a free and personal commitment.

3. Imitation goes beyond simple gestures: it encompasses an entire way of life, convictions, an attitude toward suffering and trials. In Thessalonica, the believers "became imitators of us" by receiving the Word "in the midst of much tribulation" (1 Thessalonians 1:6) — they imitated not only faith but also joyful perseverance in difficulties.
G3402.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to imitate" (mimeomai), which expresses the idea of conscious and voluntary imitation. Its root image refers to reproducing something after having observed it, like a child who watches and then mimics the gesture of a parent. This verb, and thus this noun, are always used in the New Testament to speak of commendable and moral imitation, never for false imitation or deceitful counterfeiting.
G3402.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Paul and in the epistle to the Hebrews. Paul uses it to exhort to moral and spiritual imitation: he asks the Corinthians to imitate him (1 Corinthians 4:16 and 11:1), but immediately clarifies that he himself is only an imitator of Christ — the chain always goes back to Jesus as the ultimate model. Among the Thessalonians, this word marks not only adherence to faith but also sharing in persecution (1 Thessalonians 1:6 and 2:14): to imitate is to reproduce the entire path of the model, including its sufferings. In Ephesians 5:1, it is God Himself whom we are called to imitate "as beloved children." The epistle to the Hebrews (6:12) speaks of imitating "those who, through faith and patience, inherit the promises" — a call to follow the example of the ancients in their faithfulness.
G3402.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith is not abstract or solitary: it is also learned by observing the lives of those who precede or accompany us. Imitating a faithful model strengthens our own commitment, especially when the road becomes difficult. It is also an invitation to live in such a way that others can imitate us in Christ — a gentle responsibility, that of being a small reflection of the Master for those who look to us.

sens: To bring to mind a fact, a person, an event from the past
To be aware of something at the moment one speaks or acts
To care for someone, to think of them with concern
To be recalled to memory, to come to mind
Not to forget, to retain in memory
G3403.detail:
1. To remember is to bring to mind something that one has known or experienced in the past. It is the act of memory: one recalls past events, people, spoken words. When Peter "remembered" (Matthew 26:75), he suddenly understood what he had done — he had denied Jesus — and this realization troubled him.

2. Sometimes the verb refers to the moment when something comes to mind, often suddenly or triggered by a circumstance. To the disciples who saw the offering at Jesus' feet, "it came to mind" that Scripture speaks of zeal consuming (John 2:17).

3. In certain passages, remembering a person also means to have concern for them, to think of them with kindness and to act accordingly. Paul tells Timothy that he "remembers him" which expresses his attachment and desire to see him again (2 Timothy 1:4).

4. When God "remembers" someone, it means He turns His attention to them, recalls their cries, their actions, and intervenes for them: it is the opposite of forgetting or indifference. Acts 10:31 states that Cornelius' prayer and almsgiving have been "remembered" before God.

5. The verb can also mean "to be kept in memory," "to remain in memory": this is the passive form of the verb. The disciples remembered all that Jesus had said (Luke 24:8).
G3403.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient root related to the action of holding in memory, of keeping in mind. Greek uses several forms of the verb according to the tenses: in the present "mimnéskô", in the perfect "mémnemai" (which means "I remember" and retains a nuance of stability). In the Greek Old Testament, this verb mainly translates the Hebrew "zakhar" which evokes the idea of "bringing to memory" or "taking into account." This Hebrew word, concerning God, carries a dimension of commitment: to remember is to honor a promise or a commitment.
G3403.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke, who loves to describe moments of realization. It takes several forms: sometimes the disciples or people "remember" a word or an act (John 2:17, Luke 24:8), sometimes one asks Jesus to "remember" us (Luke 23:42). Very often, it introduces a new understanding — one remembers Scripture and recognizes it applied to the present moment (John 12:16). For God, "to remember" is a strong act: He remembers mercy (Luke 1:54), He remembers prayers (Acts 10:31). In Hebrews, the verb receives a legal nuance: God "remembers no more" the forgiven sins (Hebrews 10:17), which means He has voluntarily ceased to count them. The verb can also mark benevolent concern: Paul "remembers" Timothy with affection (2 Timothy 1:4), Jesus asks the thief to "remember" Him (Luke 23:42).
G3403.portee: This word teaches that remembering is not passive: it is an act of faith and responsibility. To remember the words of Jesus is to recognize their truth at the moment when one needs it. As for God who "remembers" us, it is the guarantee that He never forgets us, that He listens to our prayers, and that He honors His promises — a tremendous comfort for the believer who doubts his worth in God's eyes.

sens: To feel an intense aversion toward someone
To reject someone with hostility
To have indifference or contempt toward something
To love less, to prefer one over another
G3404.detail:
1. To feel an intense aversion, a hostile feeling toward a person. It is the radical opposite of benevolent love. The world hates the disciples of Jesus because they do not belong to it: "the world hates you" (John 15:19).
2. To be the object of this aversion, to suffer from the rejection and hostility of others. Mark expresses it clearly: "You will be hated by all for my name's sake" (Mark 13:13), a promise that Jesus makes to His disciples.
3. To reject a practice or a way of doing things, to dismiss it as contrary to what one wants or is. Paul says: "I hate what I do" (Romans 7:15), describing the inner conflict of the sinner.
4. To prefer one over another, in the sense of loving less or neglecting one thing in favor of another. This is a weaker usage of the word: "No one can serve two masters... he will hate the one and love the other" (Matthew 6:24) means that one can truly give oneself only to one.
G3404.origine: The Greek verb μισέω comes from a root expressing aversion and rejection. In classical Greek, the word denotes personal hostility. In the Septuagint (the Greek Bible), it mainly translates the Hebrew שָׂנֵא (sānaʾ), which carries the same emotional and moral weight. The Hebrew can also, rarely, express a relative preference ("to love less"), a nuance that Greek takes up in some contexts.
G3404.emploi: The verb μισέω is used 37 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles of John. It first describes the hostility of the world toward Jesus and His disciples (John 15:18-25, 1 John 3:13): it is a consequence of unbelief and the choice to remain on the side of sin. It also expresses God's moral requirement of His people: the old Law spoke of hating one's enemy, but Jesus corrects this by teaching love even for enemies (Matthew 5:43-44). Paul uses it to describe the inner struggle: the Christian hates his own sinful acts (Romans 7:15). Finally, the word can mean a relative preference: choosing one mastery over another (Matthew 6:24, Luke 16:13).
G3404.portee: This word reveals a reality that Jesus promises to His disciples: being hated by the world is normal for those who follow Him. But it also invites moral vigilance: to love one is often to hate another — fidelity to God requires turning away from sin. And Jesus' teaching on loving enemies (Matthew 5:44) shows that even in the face of received hatred, the Christian is called to a radically different reaction.

sens: Payment of salary or reward in return for work or action
Promised or expected reward for faithfulness and obedience
Punishment or deserved penalty in return for a fault
G3405.detail: 1. The primary and concrete meaning is that of payment: a remuneration is the salary one receives for their work, the price at which one evaluates and gives what is due. It is a fair exchange: one gives something, one receives in return. 2. In the language of faith, remuneration becomes spiritual reward. Moses had "his eyes fixed on the remuneration" (Hebrews 11:26): he accepted the disgrace of Christ, convinced that God would repay him a hundredfold. This is the hope of the faithful believer. 3. However, remuneration can also be penal. "Every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution" (Hebrews 2:2): one who violates the Law suffers the consequences of their disobedience. God rewards not only faithfulness but also rebellion.
G3405.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: μισθός (misthós), the salary or price of work, and ἀποδίδωμι (apodídômi), to give back, to render what is due. Together, they convey the idea of rendering or paying according to what one has received or done. It is a compound word that expresses an act of justice: each receives according to their works.
G3405.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and it always refers to a judgment rendered by God. In Hebrews 2:2, it concerns the punishment for transgressions of the Law given by angels. In Hebrews 10:35 and 11:26, it pertains to the reward promised to those who persevere in faith. Both aspects—punishment and reward—are based on the same principle: God does not leave human actions without consequence. It is a solemn term that emphasizes the certainty of divine judgment.
G3405.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is not without consequence. God rewards each according to their works: He faithfully recompenses, whether to reward perseverance or to punish rebellion. For the believer, this means that their faithfulness will not be forgotten, and they can expect a just remuneration from God, even if it comes at a high cost in this life (as it did for Moses). For those who reject God, it is a warning: sin has a price, and it will be paid.

sens: one who gives a reward, a salary
one who recompenses works
God who rewards those who seek Him
G3406.detail: 1. The word literally designates one who pays a salary or gives a reward for work done. It is an employer or master who pays what is due to one who has served. 2. Figuratively, it refers to one who recompenses acts, efforts, or faith—who "pays back" for works. The image is that of equitable justice: each receives according to what they have done. 3. In Hebrews 11:6, the word applies to God Himself: God is the remunerator of those who sincerely seek Him. This means that God does not overlook faith and the search of the human heart, and that He rewards those who draw near to Him with true conviction.
G3406.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: "misthós" (salary, wages), "apó" (from, starting from), and "dótēs" (one who gives). Literally: "one who gives the salary." It is a rare word in Greek, formed to express the idea of divine retribution or reward. It conveys the Hebrew idea of a just God who never forgets the work of His servants.
G3406.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:6. The apostle uses it in a key passage about faith: to draw near to God and please Him, one must first believe that He exists, and then believe that He rewards those who seek Him. The context is that of the faith of the ancients (Abraham, Enoch, Noah) who all acted believing in this promise of divine reward. The word expresses one of the fundamental truths of faith: God sees, God remembers, God recompenses.
G3406.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God is not indifferent to their efforts, prayers, and sincere quest for Him. To believe that God is a remunerator is to believe that nothing is lost, that every act of faith and every sacrifice made for Him finds its meaning and reward. It is a promise that supports perseverance in faith, especially in times of doubt or spiritual fatigue.

sens: Worker hired for a job in exchange for a salary
Servant or household employee paid by the day
Figuratively: one who acts only for money, without devotion or loyalty
G3407.detail: 1. The mercenary is primarily a worker or servant hired to perform a specific task in exchange for an agreed salary. In the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:17), the young man thinks that even his father's mercenaries "have bread in abundance": these are temporary servants, paid for their services, who enjoy a material security that the son has lost by fleeing. 2. By extension, it refers to a household employee hired for a specified period, unlike a slave or servant bound for life to the family. In Luke 15:19, the repentant son asks his father: "treat me as one of your mercenaries," accepting to no longer be a son but a simple employee, as long as he is fed. 3. In a figurative and pejorative sense, the mercenary designates one who acts solely for financial interest, without heart or devotion. This connotation reflects the purely transactional nature of this type of relationship: one works for the salary, not out of love or loyalty.
G3407.origine: The Greek word misthios comes from misthós ("salary, wages"), which refers to the idea of remuneration exchanged for work. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is sâkîr (שָׂכִיר), which has the same root and meaning. The family of the Greek word also includes misthoô ("to hire, engage for wages") and misthodotés ("one who pays wages"). The image is that of a purely economic relationship: money is given in exchange for a service.
G3407.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15. The fallen son first compares himself to his father's mercenaries to highlight his destitution: he, once a son, has nothing, while these mere employees live in abundance. Then he offers to his father to treat him "as one of your mercenaries," expressing his repentance and acceptance of a humiliated condition. In both cases, the mercenary embodies one who has a contractual and temporary relationship with a household, without the status or affection reserved for family. This image reinforces the theme of the parable: the return of the son and the restoration of his filial relationship with the father.
G3407.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the difference between a purely transactional relationship and a relationship of love and grace. The prodigal son first sees himself as an unworthy mercenary, accepting to serve for bread; but his father receives him, not as an employee, but as a restored son. For the Christian, this reminds us that the relationship with God is not based on a commercial exchange (doing good to be rewarded), but on the grace of the Father who welcomes us and restores us beyond what we deserve.

sens: The payment received for work done
The retribution that comes to someone according to their deeds
The honor or benefit received from an action
The reward promised by God to those who obey Him
The spiritual advantage that the believer expects from their faithfulness
G3408.detail:
1. In its primary and concrete sense, it is the wage paid to a worker for their labor. Jesus speaks of the master of the vineyard who pays "the wage" to the workers (Matthew 20:8), and Paul reminds us that "the laborer deserves his wages" (1 Timothy 5:18). It is what one receives in return for toil.

2. More broadly, it is the retribution — what justly comes to someone in exchange for their actions. Jesus warns the hypocritical Pharisees: they "receive their reward" here on earth (Matthew 6:5), meaning that their vanity is sufficient to satisfy them.

3. It is also the honor or advantage gained through one's actions. Whoever receives a prophet or a righteous person "will not lose their reward" (Matthew 10:41), for they have participated in a holy work.

4. In the divine context, it is the heavenly reward that God promises to the faithful believer. Jesus tells the persecuted: "your reward will be great in heaven" (Matthew 5:12), like an inexhaustible wealth.

5. It is the spiritual stakes of the Christian life: each one "will receive their own reward according to their own labor" (1 Corinthians 3:8), which means that God discerns and values what we do for Him.
G3408.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of wage and payment. It often translates the Hebrew "שׂכָר" (sakhar), which has the same meaning of retribution and reward. It is a common word in commercial and legal language: it primarily denotes what is paid for a service. But gradually, the Bible enriches it: it becomes the image of divine justice — God leaves nothing without reward, and everyone will receive according to their works.
G3408.emploi: The word is used 28 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew and Paul. In its literal sense, it denotes the wage of the worker (Matthew 20:8; Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18). But its major theological meaning is divine reward. It is promised to the persecuted (Matthew 5:12), to those who give alms without ostentation (Matthew 6:1-2), to those who receive a prophet (Matthew 10:41). Paul uses it to speak of the retribution that each will receive according to their work in the Church (1 Corinthians 3:8, 3:14). It is also the motive for actions: "to have a reward" (Matthew 5:46; 1 Corinthians 9:17) means to act in order to receive something. The word can also denote a false reward — that of lies or injustice (Acts 1:18; 2 Peter 2:13, 2:15).
G3408.portee: This word reminds the believer that God leaves nothing without reward — not even a cup of water given in the name of Jesus. It frees from the idea that Christian sacrifice is in vain: persecution, renunciation, service have eternal weight in the eyes of God. But it also invites sincerity: doing good to gain the esteem of men means already having received one's reward here on earth. The true reward is that which comes from God alone, in heaven.

sens: to hire someone in exchange for a wage
to engage workers for a task or job
G3409.detail:
1. To hire means to employ: to take someone into service by promising them a wage in return. It is the action of the master of the house who "goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard" (Matthew 20:1). The master proposes an agreement: "I will hire you at such a price" (implied), and the workers agree to work for that wage.
2. The word denotes the engagement of workers to accomplish a specific and limited task. Here, the workers who are not "hired" by anyone must wait: the master comes to hire them late in the day with the order "Go also to my vineyard" (Matthew 20:7). It is a temporary work contract, based on the agreement between employer and employee.
G3409.origine: The verb hire (μισθόω) comes from the root μισθός, which means "wage" or "price of labor." The word evokes the image of a commercial agreement: giving money to receive a service. In ancient Hebrew, the word שׂכָר (sakhar, "wage") expresses the same idea: to compensate someone for their labor.
G3409.emploi: The verb hire appears twice in the New Testament, only in Matthew 20, in the parable of the workers in the vineyard. Matthew uses it to show how the master recruits workers at different hours of the day: in the morning (Matthew 20:1), then at the third, sixth, and ninth hour, and finally at the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:7). The context is that of daily paid work, and the word emphasizes the agreement between the one offering the work and the one accepting it.
G3409.portee: This parable, through the verb hire, speaks to us of God's generosity towards all who respond to His call, whether they come early or late. It reminds us that God engages us in His service and promises us a reward, not according to the time worked, but according to His grace. The word hire invites us to meditate on our relationship with God: are we ready to accept His engagement, His remuneration, and His authority?

sens: Dwelling taken on rent
Temporary accommodation obtained for payment
G3410.detail:
1. The word denotes a dwelling that one occupies in exchange for rent: it is a house that one does not own, but which one inhabits because one pays for it. In Acts 28:30, Paul "stayed two whole years in a rented house" in Rome during his captivity — a temporary lodging, as he was a prisoner under house arrest.
2. By extension, it is accommodation obtained through a rental contract, a temporary arrangement rather than ownership. The word emphasizes the provisional and paid nature of the occupation.
G3410.origine: The word comes from the root *misthōō* (to hire, to employ), which itself derives from *misthos* (wage, rent, price). The family of words evokes the idea of an exchange: one pays a price (misthos) to obtain something. In ancient Greek, *misthōma* originally meant "price of rent" or "wage"; then the meaning extended to "the thing rented itself," and particularly to "rented house." In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew *etnan* (wage, price) when it comes to payments.
G3410.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:30. It is in this specific context: Paul arrives in Rome as a prisoner awaiting judgment before the emperor. The Roman authorities allow him to live under guard, and he rents a house to live in during the two years of waiting. The context emphasizes that even in captivity, Paul enjoys a relative freedom of movement and can receive visitors. The rare Greek word for this passage shows that Luke (the author of Acts) chooses to emphasize the legal and paid arrangement of this lodging, rather than a simple dwelling.
G3410.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian's life on earth is temporary and provisional. Like Paul who stays in a rented house, we are travelers in this world, temporarily occupying our dwellings. It also invites us to see how God provides for the concrete needs of His own — even in captivity, Paul can live decently and fulfill his ministry. It is an image of trust in divine providence.

sens: worker hired for a wage
shepherd who only cares for the flock for money
person who acts solely out of self-interest, without devotion
G3411.detail:
1. A mercenary is primarily a worker hired temporarily and paid by the day or for a task. In Mark 1:20, Jesus calls His disciples to their father Zebedee, who is working with his "workers" to mend the nets: these are laborers hired for a wage.

2. The term more broadly refers to anyone who works solely to receive a wage, without personal attachment to the one who employs them. John 10:12-13 contrasts the good shepherd with the mercenary: the latter "sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees," because "he does not care for the sheep" — he thinks only of his pay, not the well-being of the flock.

3. By spiritual extension, the mercenary symbolizes one who lacks true devotion, who acts out of pure self-interest and abandons at the first sign of danger. This is the opposite image of the authentic shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep.
G3411.origine: The word comes from the Greek root *misthos* (wage, pay) and the suffix *-ōtos* which designates one who has a quality or function. A mercenary is literally one who receives a wage. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word is *sakar* (related to the idea of reward).
G3411.emploi: The term appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in Mark and John. Mark uses it in a neutral, simply descriptive sense: Zebedee's workers are employees. John makes it a central theological concept in John 10, where Jesus establishes a dramatic contrast between the mercenary and the good shepherd. This parable reveals that true spiritual service is measured not by the salary received, but by the sacrifice made for those being led.
G3411.portee: The word "mercenary" challenges Christians regarding the quality of their commitment. Are we disciples of Jesus truly attached to Him and to others, or do we serve out of opportunism? This passage calls pastors and leaders to examine themselves: do they care for the flock out of love, or only for their income or prestige? It is a measure of the heart.

sens: Main city of the island of Lesbos in the eastern Mediterranean
G3412.detail: Mytilene is the capital and most important city of the island of Lesbos, located in the eastern Mediterranean near the coast of Asia Minor. Paul arrives there during his third missionary journey, after traveling overland to Assos (Acts 20:14).
G3412.origine: The ancient Greek name was Mytilèné, which evolved into Mitulène in later texts. The island of Lesbos was famous in antiquity as a center of culture, notably for the poets Sappho and Alcaeus. Mytilene itself was an important commercial port.
G3412.emploi: Mytilene appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:14. Paul stops there on his journey to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary trip. This stop is significant as it is mentioned as an important stage in his maritime itinerary across the Mediterranean. The city was a major urban center, worthy of mention as a geographical landmark for first-century readers.

sens: The archangel
Chief of God's angels
One who fights against evil
G3413.detail: Michael is one of the most powerful angelic beings, called an archangel (that is, a first-ranking angel, chief of the angels). His name means "Who is like God?", a question that expresses his absolute fidelity to God. In Jude 1:9, we see him in conflict with the devil over the body of Moses, acting with authority but also with respect for God's judgment. In Revelation 12:7, he appears at the head of the heavenly armies, fighting the dragon (Satan) and his angels in a cosmic war. Michael is thus presented as the protector of God's interests against the powers of evil.
G3413.origine: The name Michael comes from Hebrew and literally means "Who is like God?" — a rhetorical question affirming that no one can equal God. This name reflects Michael's role: to be the defender of God's people and the champion against Satan. Michael also appears in the book of Daniel in the Old Testament as the protector of the people of Israel.
G3413.emploi: Michael is mentioned twice in the New Testament. In Jude 1:9, the apostle Jude recounts an event where Michael contends with the devil over the body of Moses, showing that even in the face of incarnate evil, Michael does not allow pride or arrogance to guide his actions — he appeals to God's judgment. In Revelation 12:7, John sees a vision of Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon and his angels in heaven, a battle that represents God's ultimate victory over Satan. These two passages emphasize his role as a faithful fighter against the powers of evil.
G3413.portee: Michael reminds believers that God has heavenly powers working for His glory and against evil. His example of authority mixed with respect for divine judgment invites Christians to combat evil without arrogance, relying on God. His promised victory over the dragon assures that evil, no matter how powerful it seems, is destined for defeat.

sens: Unit of weight or currency in antiquity
Sum of money entrusted to someone for safekeeping or profit
G3414.detail:
1. The mina is an ancient monetary unit of the Semitic and Mediterranean world, equivalent to one hundred drachmas. It served both as a weight (for weighing precious metals) and as a recognized exchange value in trade. Jesus uses it in His parable as a well-known monetary reference to His audience.
2. In the parable of the minas (Luke 19:13-25), this word refers to the money that the master entrusts to his servants before going on a journey, so that they may work with it and multiply it while he is away. Each servant receives one mina, and it is the productivity of this sum (has he increased it, decreased it, lost it?) that will determine their faithfulness.
G3414.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew mané (מָנֶה) and the Aramaic mena (מְנֵא), which literally mean "portion" or "measured part" — the idea of a defined, weighed quantity. It is a Semitic word that spread throughout the ancient Mediterranean basin. In Greek, the mina has variable values depending on the regions, but in Attica, it is worth one hundred drachmas, which are themselves subdivided into obols.
G3414.emploi: The word appears only six times in the New Testament, all in the parable of Luke 19:13-25. Jesus tells how a nobleman gives one mina to each of his ten servants with the order to "put this money to work" during his absence (v. 13). Upon his return, he asks for an account: the first servant has multiplied his mina tenfold (v. 16), the second fivefold (v. 18), but a third has simply kept it, wrapped in a cloth, out of fear (v. 20). The master praises the two productive servants and punishes the lazy one by taking away his mina to give it to the one who has ten (v. 24-25). This parable illustrates how God entrusts gifts or responsibilities to each believer and expects them to bear fruit.
G3414.portee: The mina teaches that God entrusts us with talents, resources, time — whether we are rich or poor — and that He will hold us accountable for them. It is not the absence of risk or inactivity that He rewards, but the faith put into action. Each mina entrusted challenges: what are you doing with what God has given you? Are you hiding your gifts out of fear, or are you deploying them to bear fruit for His kingdom?

sens: Christian disciple from Cyprus
Host of the Apostle Paul
G3416.detail: Mnason is a man from the island of Cyprus who converted to Jesus Christ and has lived there for a long time: he is referred to as an "old disciple" in the only verse where the Bible mentions him. During the Apostle Paul's journey to Jerusalem, the other disciples from Caesarea bring him to Mnason so that Paul and his companions can find lodging there (Acts 21:16). This is a simple yet beautiful example of Christian hospitality: this brother makes his home available to the servants of God on their journey.
G3416.origine: The name Mnason comes from Greek and literally means "one who remembers" or "one who thinks of," related to the Greek root *mnē-* which expresses memory. It is a classical Greek name, common in the Hellenistic world.
G3416.emploi: Mnason appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 21:16. The Apostle Paul, returning to Jerusalem after his third missionary journey, stays at his home. The text refers to him as an "old disciple," which means he has believed in Jesus for a long time, likely since one of the early waves of the Gospel in the Mediterranean. His presence reveals how the early Church was well-rooted in the Mediterranean islands, and how Christians supported one another in their travels.
G3416.portee: Mnason illustrates the virtue of hospitality that is dear to the heart of the New Testament: welcoming the servants of God and brothers in faith. His gesture, though brief, shows that every Christian, in humility, has a role to play in God's plan by putting their resources at the service of others.

sens: The act of speaking about someone or something, of bringing it to mind by word
The act of remembering, keeping in memory
The act of praying for someone or something
The act of recalling, keeping present in mind
G3417.detail:
1. This word primarily denotes the act of speaking about someone, naming them, bringing them to mind: Paul says that he makes "mention" of his correspondents in his conversations or writings, as in Romans 1:9 where he states he constantly makes "mention" of the Romans.
2. It also means to remember, to keep someone in one's heart and thoughts: this active remembrance vivifies the relationship, as shown in Philippians 1:3 where Paul gives thanks "for all the remembrance" he has of the Philippians.
3. Especially in the context of Pauline letters, "making mention" of someone in prayers means to pray for them in a named and conscious manner, as in 1 Thessalonians 1:2 and Ephesians 1:16 where the Apostle "makes mention" of his brothers in his prayers to God.
4. It can also be the act of keeping someone in memory constantly, keeping them present in one's thoughts: in 1 Thessalonians 3:6, the Thessalonians "have" a good remembrance of Paul, meaning he remains alive in their hearts.
G3417.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to remember," and it denotes the action of remembering or putting that remembrance into words. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the root "zakhar" (זָכַר) which means both "to remember" and "to mention." It is a word of memory and relationship, linking the inner act of remembrance to its outer expression.
G3417.emploi: Paul uses this word seven times, mainly in his letters, always to speak of his own remembrance of the Churches or the people to whom he writes. It appears primarily in three expressions: "making mention of someone" (Romans 1:9, Ephesians 1:16, 1 Thessalonians 1:2, Philemon 1:4), generally in a context of prayer and gratitude; "having a remembrance" of someone (1 Thessalonians 3:6, 2 Timothy 1:3), to express that one keeps someone present in memory and affection. The word thus expresses the continuity of the personal and spiritual bond between Paul and his correspondents, even at a distance.
G3417.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that remembering someone in prayer is a concrete and powerful form of love and faithfulness. Paul does not simply say that he thinks of the Thessalonians or the Philippians: he says that he makes "mention" of them to God, that he names them, keeping them alive in his intercession. This shows that Christian remembrance is not mere nostalgia, but an act of prayer, a way of honoring those we love and entrusting them to God.

sens: Place where a dead person is buried, funerary monument
Place hollowed out of rock to receive a body
Figure of death and corruption
G3418.detail:
1. A sepulcher is a building or place intended to receive the body of a dead person — it is the tomb where the deceased are buried. In the Gospels, Jesus is laid in "a sepulcher hewn out of the rock, where no one had yet been laid" (Luke 23:53): it is a burial chamber carved into the stone, a sign of respect and wealth.
2. The sepulcher can also simply refer to the burial place, the chosen spot to place the body. The women come to the sepulcher on the morning of the resurrection to anoint Jesus, showing that they know the exact location (Luke 24:1).
3. Sometimes, the word takes on a figurative sense: it symbolizes death itself, corruption, and nothingness. A man possessed by demons had "his dwelling among the sepulchers" (Luke 8:27) — an image of a life bound to death and destruction.
G3418.origine: The Greek word mnēma comes from the root mnaomai ("to remember"), as a sepulcher is also a memorial, a monument that keeps the memory of the dead alive. It translates the Hebrew qèbèr (grave, sepulcher) and reflects Jewish burial practices, where burial in a hewn or constructed tomb was the customary rite.
G3418.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily denotes the tomb of Jesus: the women visit it after the resurrection, Joseph of Arimathea lays the body there, and the disciples keep its memory. It is also found in Luke in the story of the demoniac of Gerasa, who lived among the sepulchers — a stark image of satanic bondage. Finally, Peter mentions the sepulcher of David (Acts 2:29) as proof that David is truly dead, unlike the risen Christ. The word always signifies a material place, a construction or cavity intended for burial.
G3418.portee: The sepulcher reminds the believer that death is a formidable and definitive reality — except for Jesus alone, who emerged alive from it. It is a sign of Christian hope: while David "is buried and his sepulcher is still with us," Jesus has conquered death and left the sepulcher. For the disciple, meditating on the empty tomb of Christ is to affirm his victory over the last enemy.

sens: a structure or excavation intended to bury a dead person
a tomb carved into rock or a place where a corpse rests
a funerary monument or commemorative building
G3419.detail:
1. The tomb is primarily a physical place, underground or monumental, where the body of a deceased person is placed. It is a grave, often carved into rock (Matthew 27:60 describes the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, hewn from the rock). The word concretely designates this structure where the dead rest.

2. More broadly, it refers to any place, natural or constructed, where human remains lie. In Galilee, demoniacs lived "coming out of the tombs" (Mark 5:2), caves or abandoned graves. This shows that the tomb can be a cavern or a space carved into a cliff.

3. The word also takes on a figurative sense of "monument" or "memorial." Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for building and adorning the tombs of the prophets (Matthew 23:29): here, it is an act of commemoration, of recognition, but which hides spiritual forgetfulness.
G3419.origine: The Greek μνημεῖον comes from the root μνή- (mnē-), which means "memory," "remembrance." A tomb is therefore literally a place of memory — it is remembered and marked. The Hebrew word קֶבֶר (qéber), which it often translates, has the same concrete meaning: a grave, a burial place. The Greek word emphasizes the memorial aspect: the tomb keeps alive the memory of the deceased.
G3419.emploi: The word appears 37 times in the New Testament, mainly in the four Gospels and Acts. It first designates the caves or tombs where the possessed lived (Matthew 8:28, Mark 5:2), then the tomb of Jesus after the crucifixion — this place recurs constantly: the women go there, Peter and John run there, one goes in and out (Luke 24:9; John 20:2-11). Some uses broaden the meaning: Jesus' reproach to the Pharisees for "building the tombs of the prophets" (Matthew 23:29) is a moral critique, a reminder that honoring the memory of the dead does not prevent malice towards the living. The word remains very concrete in the Bible, centered on the tomb as a physical and memorial place.
G3419.portee: The tomb, in the Gospels, is never neutral: it is the place where death reigns and where Christ triumphs. The women come there to weep for Jesus, but they find resurrection there — the Gospel redefines the meaning of the tomb, shifting from a place of definitive end to a place of transition to life. For the believer, it is a call to recognize that death no longer has the final word.

sens: The act of remembering, keeping in memory
The trace that a person or event leaves in the mind
G3420.detail: 1. Remembrance is the act of keeping a person, a word, or a past event present in one's mind. It is memory in action, the moment when one recalls. In 2 Peter 1:15, Peter says he will make every effort so that his readers can constantly remember the truths he has taught them — the emphasis is on the act of recalling, of reviving memory. 2. By extension, remembrance also refers to what remains in us of a person or thing — the lasting imprint it leaves. It is less about the act of remembering than the very content of that memory, the living presence of the past in the present.
G3420.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb μνάομαι (to remember), which expresses the action of keeping something in one's mind. In Hebrew, words like זֵכֶר (zeker, remembrance) and זִכְרוֹן (zikron, memorial) convey the same idea, that of keeping alive the memory of a person or a covenant. Remembrance, in the Bible, is never passive: it is a voluntary action that maintains the relationship with the past.
G3420.emploi: This word appears only once in 2 Peter 1:15, where Peter uses the expression "make remembrance" to say that he will ensure his disciples keep his teachings in memory after his death. The apostle recognizes that remembrance has a vital function: it perpetuates the transmission of truth between generations and keeps the teaching alive for those who need it.
G3420.portee: For the Christian, this word emphasizes the importance of actively cultivating the memory of the truths of faith and the teachings received. It is a call not to let fade what has transformed our lives, but to regularly remember it so that it continues to guide and shape us. The conscious memory of the message of the Gospel is a spiritual discipline that nourishes our walk with God.

sens: To bring to mind, to recall
To have in memory, to keep the memory of
To think of, not to forget someone or something
To evoke, to mention
G3421.detail:
1. To remember is to bring to mind what one has known or learned in the past. It is an act of memory, a rising of the past into present consciousness. Jesus asks his disciples: "Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand?" (Matthew 16:9), inviting them to mentally recall this miracle they witnessed.

2. To keep in memory is to preserve the trace of a person or event in one's heart and mind, without forgetting. When it says "remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you" (Hebrews 13:7), it invites to keep alive the memory of these spiritual leaders and their teaching.

3. To think of someone is to hold them present in one's mind with intention and affection. Paul writes to the Colossians: "Remember my chains" (Colossians 4:18), calling them to keep him in thought during his captivity and to pray for him.

4. To mention is to evoke or speak of something. When one remembers, one can also mention it to others, as a form of reminder or shared testimony.
G3421.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to be attentive" or "to be aware." It is related to the Greek word "mnémè" (memory) and the Hebrew root "zakhar" (to remember, to keep in memory), which it often translates in the Greek Old Testament. The basic idea is one of presence in the mind, an attention of the heart directed towards the past or towards someone absent.
G3421.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Epistle to the Hebrews, with interesting nuances. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, John, Luke), it expresses the recall of past events or taught words: Jesus invites his disciples to remember his miracles or his prophetic words. In Paul, the verb takes on a relational dimension: to remember someone is to hold them in thought with affection or intercession (Colossians 4:18, 1 Thessalonians 1:3). In Hebrews, to remember becomes a spiritual act: to remember spiritual leaders is to imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). The verb can have an object (the person or thing being remembered) or be absolute (simply to remember).
G3421.portee: Biblically, to remember is never a simple mental act: it is a form of faithfulness and obedience. When Jesus commands "remember my word," he calls his disciples to a commitment to his teachings. When Paul asks to be remembered in chains, he invites practical intercession. To remember God or his word is to remain faithful to the covenant and the promises. For the Christian, this verb is an invitation to keep alive the teachings received, the examples of faith encountered, and to let the past transform the present.

sens: What keeps alive the memory of a person or an action
An act or an offering that is remembered before God
A lasting testimony that transcends time
G3422.detail:
1. A memory is what perpetuates the remembrance of a person or what they have done, so that it is spoken of long after. When the woman anoints Jesus with perfume, he promises that her act will be told wherever the Gospel is proclaimed — it is an eternal memory that is promised to her (Matthew 26:13, Mark 14:9).
2. A memory can also be an offering or a prayer that rises before God and of which he remembers. The prayers and alms of Cornelius have ascended as a memory before God (Acts 10:4), meaning they have drawn his attention and have been received by him.
3. This word evokes the idea that an act of faithfulness or love leaves a permanent mark — not only in the memory of men but also in that of God, and determines the future of the one who performs it.
G3422.origine: The word comes from the Greek root μνήμ- (mnêm-) which means "to remember," "to have in mind." Greek uses it to translate the Hebrew זֵכֶר (zéker) and its derivatives, which denote the memory that is perpetuated of a person or an action. The Hebrew root expresses the idea that a name or a work endures in the memory and in the action of God.
G3422.emploi: This word appears three times in the New Testament. It is used twice by Jesus himself (in Matthew and Mark) when he affirms that the woman's act of love will be perpetuated in memory. A third time, Peter uses it to describe how the prayers and alms of Cornelius have ascended as a memory before God. In all cases, it refers to acts of devotion or love whose remembrance persists — either among men, or before God, or in both. The word does not simply denote a passive memory, but rather a lasting mark that inspires and that God honors.
G3422.portee: This word assures us that our acts of faith, love, and generosity do not fade into oblivion: they leave a memory before God and touch others. It invites the believer to understand that God remembers and does not leave without effect what is done out of love for him or for others. This gives an eternal depth to each of our gestures, even the humblest.

sens: to promise in marriage, to unite by a marriage commitment
to be betrothed (for the woman)
G3423.detail:
1. This verb denotes the act of promising two people to each other in marriage — an official engagement, often arranged in biblical times, that unites two families before the wedding ceremony itself. This is what happened to Mary and Joseph: even before living together, Joseph had betrothed Mary, meaning he had solemnly committed to marry her (Matthew 1:18, Luke 1:27). In the passive form (for the woman), the verb simply means "to be betrothed" — it is the state of one who is awaiting her marriage: Luke 2:5 describes Mary as "his betrothed," that of Joseph, awaiting the event she carries within her.

2. In the Jewish world of that time, being betrothed was a very serious official status: breaking off an engagement was a grave act. The word translates an engagement before the actual marriage, a promise that binds the two families together.
G3423.origine: This Greek verb comes from a root related to marriage and promise. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding verb evoked the action of "betrothing" someone, establishing a promised marital bond. The term belongs to the family of words that speak of marital union, of what binds two people to each other.
G3423.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the first two chapters of Matthew and Luke — in both forms. In the active form, it describes the action of Joseph who had betrothed Mary (Matthew 1:18). In the passive form, it describes the state of Mary herself, "betrothed" to Joseph (Luke 1:27 and 2:5). All three occurrences concern the birth of Jesus and Mary's marital status before childbirth. The context shows that betrothals truly existed, with legal weight: it is because of this betrothal bond that Joseph and Mary were considered bound to each other.
G3423.portee: This word reminds the reader that Jesus was born in a normal human setting: that of a family established by marriage, according to the customs of the time. It also highlights the delicacy of Mary's situation — she was legally promised to Joseph but pregnant before the marriage was consummated, creating a tension that could only be resolved by the revelation of the action of the Holy Spirit. This detail anchors the incarnation of Jesus in human and familial reality.

sens: one who has difficulty forming words
one whose speech is hindered, who expresses themselves with difficulty
G3424.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has difficulty speaking, whose voice does not come out easily — it is the image of speech that "stumbles" or falters. In Mark 7:32, it is a deaf man who, due to his deafness, cannot articulate sounds well: his difficulty in speaking is linked to his inability to hear and imitate speech.
2. More broadly, the word evokes any obstacle that hinders expression: an injury, a malformation, or simply a lack of training. It is a state of communicational weakness, not a total absence of speech, but rather laborious and strained speech.
G3424.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "mogis" (with difficulty, barely) and "lalos" (speaking, talkative). It literally paints someone whose speech comes out with difficulty, who speaks "barely." It is a rare word in ancient Greek; the Bible borrows it to describe a speech impairment. In Isaiah 35:6 (in the Greek translation of the Old Testament), a Hebrew word meaning "mute" is rendered this way, suggesting a continuum: from complete silence to hindered speech.
G3424.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 7:32. Jesus heals a man who has two disabilities: he is deaf and his speech is difficult. The fact that Mark uses this precise word shows that deafness has affected his ability to speak normally — he cannot reproduce the sounds he does not hear. It is a case of total healing: after Jesus has opened his ears, we learn later (v. 35) that his tongue is loosed and he speaks correctly. The word thus paints a concrete physical and communicational reality, not merely a temporary slowness or stuttering.
G3424.portee: This healing reminds the reader that Jesus is not unaware of any form of human suffering — neither deafness nor the communication obstacles that arise from it. For the Christian, it is an image of restoration: where silence and difficulty reigned, Jesus creates clarity and the ability to communicate, to be heard, to enter into relationship. It is also a sign of his authority: he remedies what seemed irreparable.

sens: With difficulty, with a lot of effort
With great difficulty, almost hardly, as if despite resistance
Refers to something that occurs or concludes laboriously
G3425.detail:
1. The word describes an action or state that requires a lot of effort or pain to achieve. It conveys the image of a struggle, a resistance that must be overcome. In Luke 9:39, the demon causes him to foam and "has difficulty leaving him": the evil spirit struggles to let him go, as if it must forcibly tear its prey away.
2. More broadly, "barely" expresses the difficulty or slowness with which something is accomplished: not a refusal, but a laborious effort to achieve the result. The demon eventually leaves, but "barely", so tenacious is its grip.
G3425.origine: The word comes from the Greek μόγος (mogos) which means "pain, labor, hard work". It is an adverb formed from this root that evokes the idea of effort and physical or moral difficulty. The same root appears in other Greek words related to hard work and fatigue.
G3425.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:39. This unique usage is found in the account of the son tormented by a mute spirit: the demon agitates him, convulses him, makes him foam, and "has difficulty leaving him" after having shattered him. The context is that of the demon's power over a child, showing the violence of its grip and the difficulty of being freed — until Jesus intervenes and casts it out.
G3425.portee: This word reminds the reader of the concrete reality of spiritual warfare and the power of evil over those it possesses. It also shows that deliverance from demonic influence is not instantaneous or easy, but requires divine intervention. It is an invitation to recognize the seriousness of possession and the greatness of the salvation that Jesus brings in the face of these dark powers.

sens: Cylindrical container used to measure grains and liquids
Image of something small, narrow, that limits or suffocates light
G3426.detail:
1. The bushel is a wooden or clay container, the size of a basket, used in the ancient world to measure and store grains, flours, or other dry bulk materials — a common unit of volume in markets. It is an everyday object that every listener knows well.
2. In the three Gospel passages, Jesus uses the bushel as an image of an obstacle: putting a lit lamp under a bushel prevents it from shining, stifling its radiance. In Matthew 5:15, Mark 4:21, and Luke 11:33, this image illustrates the absurdity of hiding light — just as one would not place a lamp in a secret place or under this container, but rather place it on a lampstand so that it lights up the whole house.
G3426.origine: The Greek word *modios* refers to a measuring container whose name probably comes from the Latin *modius*, itself borrowed from Greek. It is a concrete word, drawn directly from the rural and commercial life of the Mediterranean basin. It has no direct equivalent in Hebrew or Aramaic, as it was a Greek and Roman measure. The word appears only in the Greek Gospels of the New Testament, never in the Old Testament.
G3426.emploi: The word *modios* appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the first three Gospels, and always to report Jesus' teaching about the lamp. In Matthew 5:15, he speaks of those who light a lamp and do not put it under the bushel; in Mark 4:21 and Luke 11:33, the same teaching is repeated with the same terms. Each time, it is an argument of absurdity: no one lights a lamp to hide it. The context is clearly moral and spiritual — the "lamp" represents the light of faith, works, or the Word, which must not remain hidden.
G3426.portee: This image of the bushel invites the believer not to let their faith, testimony, or the gifts they have received remain stifled or unused. Jesus calls for visibility, transparency, that the light received be generously shared with those around us. It is a concrete call to the responsibility of the disciple in the world.

sens: Marital infidelity, sexual relations outside of marriage
One who commits adultery
Characterized by adultery, infidelity
Spiritual infidelity, breaking of covenant with God
G3428.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the act of marital infidelity itself: a married woman who has sexual relations with a man other than her husband is guilty of adultery (Romans 7:3 explains this precisely: a woman becomes "an adulteress" by taking another husband while the first is still alive).
2. It applies to the person who commits this act, man or woman: James 4:4 calls Christians who love the world rather than God "adulterers", borrowing the image of marital infidelity.
3. As an adjective, it qualifies what belongs to or characterizes adultery: "an adulterous generation" (Matthew 12:39, Mark 8:38) refers to a generation marked by infidelity, betrayal of divine values.
4. Figuratively, adultery becomes an image of spiritual infidelity: loving the world is committing a form of adultery against God, who has bound us by covenant, like a husband and wife.
G3428.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing a violated marital union: it is constructed on the basis of "marital bed" (lechos) with a prefix indicating alteration or change. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses words like "naaph" (to commit adultery) to describe the violation of the marital covenant; the Greek μοιχαλίς translates this reality of rupture and betrayal in the context of the New Testament.
G3428.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, almost always in a context of moral or spiritual judgment. Matthew and Mark use it to qualify the "generation" contemporary to Jesus (Matthew 12:39, 16:4; Mark 8:38): this is not an accusation of adultery in the strictly marital sense, but a global condemnation of spiritual infidelity, the refusal to believe in Jesus despite the signs of the Kingdom. Romans 7:3 uses it in the literal, legal sense to explain the law of marriage. James 4:4 metaphorically applies the term to believers who allow themselves to be seduced by the worldly system, calling them "adulterers" as if they were betraying their spiritual union with God. In 2 Peter 2:14, the "adulterer" (in the sense of the act) characterizes false teachers and their lusts. The word thus oscillates between its literal meaning (violation of marriage) and its figurative application (infidelity toward God).
G3428.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the covenant with God carries an intimacy comparable to marriage: betraying God by loving the world is a form of infidelity. It invites vigilance: love for the world is presented not as a mere distraction, but as a breaking of covenant. For one who faces the reality of marital adultery, the word emphasizes the moral and spiritual gravity of this act, which wounds not only one's spouse but also one's commitment before God.

sens: To have a sexual relationship outside of marriage or with a married person
For a man: to take a woman other than his wife
For a woman: to take a man other than her husband
Figuratively: to betray, to be unfaithful to a commitment
G3429.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to have an illicit sexual relationship that goes against the marriage covenant. It is a violation of the marital bond, whether by taking a lover or a mistress. Jesus uses this verb in Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 to say that whoever marries a divorced woman "commits adultery," because in God's eyes the first marriage still stands.
2. For a man, this specifically means taking another woman besides his own. Mark 10:11 records Jesus' words: "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery."
3. For a woman, it similarly means taking another husband. Mark 10:12 shows that the word also applies to a woman who leaves her husband: "she commits adultery."
4. In the Old Testament, the prophet Jeremiah uses this word figuratively for Israel: the people "commit adultery" against God by turning to idols, like an unfaithful wife.
G3429.origine: The Greek verb μοιχάω comes from a root that evokes the breaking of the marital bond. In Hebrew, the verb נָאַף (naap) means the same thing. This root appears in ancient biblical contexts to describe any marital infidelity. The word belongs to the moral and legal vocabulary of marriage, common to many ancient cultures.
G3429.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the words of Jesus reported by Matthew and Mark, concerning marriage and divorce. In Matthew 5:32, Jesus teaches that whoever divorces his wife without just cause exposes her to commit adultery, and whoever marries her commits adultery. In Matthew 19:9 and Mark 10:11, the same word is repeated more precisely. Mark 10:12 expands the teaching: a woman also commits adultery if she leaves her husband for another. The context is always that of marriage, divorce, and marital fidelity.
G3429.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us of the importance of the marital bond in God's eyes. Jesus condemns not only adultery itself but also the situations that lead to it, such as divorce without just cause. The word applies equally to all, men and women, with moral equality. It invites the believer to view marriage not as a revocable contract at will, but as a covenant that only death can break.

sens: Sexual relationship between a married person and someone other than their spouse
Violation of the marriage commitment
Sin and transgression of divine law
Moral impurity and corruption of the heart
G3430.detail:
1. Adultery is primarily the concrete act: an illicit sexual relationship involving a person engaged in marriage. John 8:3 shows a woman "caught in adultery," meaning caught in the act.

2. The word also designates the sin of violating the marital bond. This is why Matthew 15:19 lists adultery among the evils that come from the heart, alongside murders, thefts, and slanders: it is a serious moral evil.

3. For biblical authors, adultery is not only a private infidelity but a transgression against God Himself, who established the marriage covenant. It is a rupture of both spiritual and relational order.

4. Adultery corrupts the heart and expresses its lust: it reveals the disordered desires that inhabit the soul. Mark 7:22 mentions it in a list of disorders that defile a person.
G3430.origine: The Greek word μοιχεία comes from a root that means "to mix" or "to defile." The verb μοιχεύω (to commit adultery) appears throughout the New Testament with this same family of meanings. In Hosea and Jeremiah, the Hebrew word נָאַף designates physical adultery but also, metaphorically, the spiritual infidelity of the people towards God (like an unfaithful wife).
G3430.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament. It is found in two lists of sins: that of Matthew 15:19 (where Jesus enumerates what defiles a person, which comes from the heart) and that of Mark 7:21-22 (a parallel version with variations). John 8:3 provides the only concrete account, the episode of the woman caught in adultery brought to Jesus. Galatians 5:19 places adultery among the "works of the flesh." In all cases, the word denotes a serious violation of moral and divine order, without distinction as to whether the act is past or habitual.
G3430.portee: Adultery calls the Christian to fidelity and purity of heart, not by an external law but through inner renewal. Jesus Himself shows that it is not primarily the act that defiles, but the thought and desire oriented towards evil; hence the call to repentance and grace, even for those who have committed this sin. It is an opportunity to understand that God's forgiveness is greater than condemnation.

sens: To have sexual relations with someone other than one's spouse
To be found guilty of marital betrayal
To betray God by worshiping idols
G3431.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to have a sexual relationship with someone other than one's husband or wife, which violates the commitment made in marriage. Jesus teaches that even carnal desire constitutes a form of adultery in God's eyes (Matthew 5:28: "Anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.")
2. The word also designates the guilt and condemnation that result: whoever commits adultery becomes an adulterer, a transgressor of divine law. Paul cites it among the fundamental commandments (Romans 2:22: "You commit adultery!"), on the same level as not stealing or killing.
3. The Bible uses this word figuratively for idolatry: worshiping other gods is presented as infidelity towards God, comparable to marital infidelity. Revelation (2:22) speaks of "committing adultery" in a spiritual sense when one turns away from the living God.
G3431.origine: The Greek word comes from μοιχός (moichós), which designates the adulterer, the unfaithful. It is a classic verbal formation: the verb "to do" or "to commit" applied to the name of the reprehensible act. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses נָאַף (nā'áf), which has the same precise meaning. This continuity shows that marital fidelity is a stable principle of biblical revelation, from the Decalogue to the epistles of the New Testament.
G3431.emploi: The verb appears 12 times in the New Testament, especially in the teachings of Jesus and in the apostolic epistles. It is cited as one of the ten commandments (Matthew 5:27, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9, James 2:11), which reminds us of its importance in Mosaic law. Jesus intensifies the commandment by including the lustful gaze (Matthew 5:28), not just the physical act. The verb is also used in the passive voice, describing the woman who finds herself in this situation of transgression (Matthew 5:32, John 8:4). Figuratively, it expresses spiritual unfaithfulness: idolatry is called adultery (Revelation 2:22), which shows that human marriage reflects the covenant relationship between God and His people.
G3431.portee: This word confronts the believer with God's holiness regarding marriage and sexuality. By expanding sin beyond the physical act to include the desires of the heart, Jesus reveals that God judges intentions, not just actions. It is a call to deep moral purity and true fidelity. For the disciple, understanding adultery as a rupture of the marital covenant also helps to grasp how idolatry wounds God: one cannot serve two masters.

sens: One who commits adultery, who has a sexual relationship with a woman other than his wife
One who breaks the marriage bond through infidelity
Figuratively: one who turns away from God or His covenant by turning to idols or the world
G3432.detail:
1. Adultery refers to a man who has sexual relations outside of his marriage, with a woman who is not his wife. It is a violation of the marital bond and of God's command. In Luke 18:11, the Pharisee boasts that he is not an adulterer, which shows that it was a serious and common sin.

2. More broadly, adultery refers to any man who breaks his commitment to his wife. The term applies to one who has chosen infidelity. In Hebrews 13:4, God promises to judge adulterers: it is an act condemned by God Himself.

3. In the Bible, infidelity toward God or His covenant is sometimes described with the same imagery as marital infidelity. In James 4:4, believers who love the world are called "adulterers" because they have abandoned their faithfulness to God to turn to something else. It is an image of spiritual infidelity.
G3432.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing mixing or violation. It designates one who mixes what should not be mixed: his relationships outside of marriage. In Hebrew, the word נָאַף (naaph) has the same connotation: it is a violation of the order that God has established. The Greek form exactly captures this sense of breaking a sacred bond.
G3432.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to refer to men who commit adultery. In Luke 18:11, the Pharisee mentions it among the serious sins of which he boasts he is not guilty. In 1 Corinthians 6:9 and Hebrews 13:4, the Apostle Paul places adultery among the sins that exclude one from the kingdom of God or provoke divine judgment. In James 4:4, the word takes on a spiritual nuance: believers attached to the world are called "adulterers" against God, as if they were betraying Him by placing their affection elsewhere. The meaning remains that of serious infidelity, whether marital or toward God.
G3432.portee: This word reminds us that marriage is a sacred covenant before God, and that breaking it is a serious act that undermines the order created by God. For the believer, it is also an invitation to examine our own faithfulness: are we faithful to our covenant with God, or are we turning to the world like an adulterer seeking elsewhere what he should seek from his wife? Adultery is listed among the sins that exclude from the kingdom, which shows the severity with which the Bible judges this infidelity.

sens: with difficulty, effort
hardly, difficulty in accomplishing
scarcely, hardly, only just
G3433.detail: 1. Barely means "with great difficulty" or "just barely." It expresses that an action has been accomplished, but with pain, effort, or obstacle. In Acts 14:18, the apostles "barely" restrain the crowd from sacrificing to them, meaning they have difficulty convincing them. 2. The word can also emphasize that something occurs "just barely" or "with great difficulty": it expresses a limit just crossed or an action accomplished by a narrow margin. In Acts 27:8, the ship approaches the island "barely," meaning not without risk and difficulty. 3. Sometimes, barely marks the rare or improbable nature of an action: one can hardly imagine that it happens. In Romans 5:7, Paul says that barely anyone dies for a righteous person, meaning that it is extremely rare.
G3433.origine: The Greek word μόλις comes from an ancient root (μόλος) meaning "work, fatigue." It is thus a way of saying that an action is accomplished, but at the cost of pain, effort. It is a post-Homeric term, meaning it developed after the epics of Homer. It is close to other Greek forms expressing difficulty.
G3433.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and the epistles. In Acts, it describes the material difficulties encountered during travels: the arduous navigation (Acts 27:7-8, 16), the difficult handling of a small boat. In Romans 5:7 and 1 Peter 4:18, it appears in theological reasoning: Paul uses it to express that no one or almost no one is willing to die for a righteous person; Peter, to emphasize that the salvation of the righteous is obtained with great difficulty. The word thus expresses both physical pain and moral or spiritual difficulty.
G3433.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life, like life in general, involves difficulties and obstacles. When the New Testament says that the righteous are saved "barely," it wants to show that salvation in Christ does not come without struggle, without effort of faith, and that our perseverance must be serious. It is an invitation not to rely on ease, but to arm ourselves with courage in trials.

sens: pagan deity worshiped by the Ammonites
god to whom child sacrifices were offered
G3434.detail:
1. Moloch was the principal god of the Ammonite people, a neighboring nation to Israel. The name literally means "king" in Hebrew, but it was deliberately distorted to express disgust: it was vocalized as "Bosheth" ("shame"), just as Baal was called "the shame." 
2. This god was known and feared for the bloody practices of his cult: his worshipers offered him human sacrifices, particularly children, by passing them through fire. It was this abominable cult that the Law of Israel formally prohibited.
G3434.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew מֶלֶךְ (melek), which means "king." The biblical scribes deliberately altered its pronunciation by adding the vowels of the word בֺּשֶׁת (bosheth), "shame," to mark their condemnation of this demonic cult. Moloch was among the false gods worshiped by the neighboring peoples of Israel, such as Baal and Remphan.
G3434.emploi: Moloch appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:43, where Stephen cites the prophet Amos to reproach the leaders of Israel for their infidelity. Stephen reminds them that, despite God's miracles in the desert, their ancestors worshiped Moloch and other idols, even carrying his sacred tent in their camp. This reference illustrates how Israel, throughout its history, sometimes turned away from the true God to adopt the abominable cults of surrounding peoples.
G3434.portee: The name of Moloch in the Bible warns us about the danger of idolatry: it distances us from God and can lead us to monstrous acts, contrary to all humanity. This god represents the extent of the sin of nations without God and reminds the believer of the importance of remaining faithful to the true God rather than being seduced by the false religions of the world.

sens: To make impure or dirty by altering the purity or whiteness of something
To harm the moral or spiritual purity of a person
To compromise oneself by committing an action contrary to one's faith or consecration
G3435.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the action of staining or soiling: in Revelation 3:4, the white garments that have not been defiled maintain their shining purity, an image of garments that remain unblemished despite the surrounding dirt.
2. It also means to harm moral or spiritual purity, particularly that of the conscience. In 1 Corinthians 8:7, the weak conscience of a Christian is defiled when he eats meat sacrificed to idols because he still sees it as linked to idol worship: his heart is tainted with doubt and guilt.
3. The meaning extends to compromising oneself through actions contrary to one's consecration. In Revelation 14:4, not being defiled with women means maintaining complete integrity and fidelity, without mixing with anything that would divert from exclusive devotion to the Lord.
G3435.origine: The verb μολύνω comes from a root expressing the idea of stain or dirt. It is close to the verb μιαίνω (miainō), which also means to defile or contaminate, but μολύνω emphasizes more the alteration of the whiteness or purity of a surface. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew verbs like טָבַל (to dip, immerse) and גָּאַל (to defile), words related to concrete acts of contamination.
G3435.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always with a figurative and spiritual meaning, never concrete. In 1 Corinthians 8:7, it describes the damage to the conscience of one who acts against his religious conviction. In Revelation 3:4 and 14:4, Paul and then John use it to speak of preserving spiritual purity in the face of worldly compromises: to remain white and unblemished is to refuse moral and religious stains that could tarnish one's consecration to Christ. The context is always one of spiritual faithfulness or unfaithfulness.
G3435.portee: This word invites the Christian to be aware of the fragility of his spiritual purity and the ease with which the conscience can be tainted by compromises, even small ones. It reminds that holiness is not an isolated quality, but a constant vigilance against influences that stain the soul. It is a call not to defile one's moral integrity and devotion to Christ, and to walk worthily, dressed in white, in the presence of the Lord.

sens: State or action of making impure, of morally or spiritually soiling
Impurity contracted by contact with what is forbidden or profane
G3436.detail:
1. Defilement is the state of what has been made impure or contaminated. In 2 Corinthians 7:1, Paul exhorts believers to cleanse themselves from all "defilement of flesh and spirit," that is, from everything that has made them impure through sin or contact with evil — whether it be carnal passions or ideas contrary to God. The word evokes the image of a stain or dirt that soils and pollutes.
