2. Defilement can also specifically refer to the impurity contracted by transgression or contact with what is prohibited. It is an affront to the ritual and moral purity that the believer must wash away to regain communion with God.
G3436.origine: The word comes from the verb μολύνω (molúnô), which literally means "to soil" or "to stain." The root evokes the physical action of covering with mud or filth. In the Greek Old Testament, this word sometimes translates the Hebrew חֲנֻפָה (hanoufa), which denotes hypocrisy and moral corruption. The noun μολυσμός thus expresses both physical dirtiness and moral or spiritual impurity.
G3436.emploi: The word μολυσμός appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 7:1. Paul uses it in a context of exhortation to holiness: after reminding the Corinthians of God's promises (that He will be their God and they will be His people), he calls them to purify themselves from all defilement — both carnal (the impurities of body and passions) and spiritual (the impurities of spirit and thought). This passage shows that defilement is not simply a passive state, but something from which the believer must actively free himself to move toward sanctification.
G3436.portee: This word reminds the believer that he can be contaminated by sin and evil, but also that he has the power and duty to purify himself. The call to "cleanse oneself from all defilement" is not a judgment of condemnation, but an invitation to freedom and holiness. In Christ, the believer is not a resigned victim of his impurities: he can leave them behind and progress toward a life dedicated to God.

sens: Reproach addressed to someone for an action or word that is disapproved
Subject of discontent or grievance between people
G3437.detail:
1. The word designates a reproach, a criticism directed at someone. It is when you tell someone: "you have acted wrongly" or "I have something to reproach you for." In Colossians 3:13, Paul speaks of those who have "cause to complain" against one another — that is, legitimate reasons to reproach something to their brother or sister.
2. More broadly, it is any grievance or reason for discontent between two people. This can arise from a hurtful word, an unjust action, or an unfulfilled promise. It is what creates tensions and divisions within a community.
G3437.origine: The word comes from the verb μέμφομαι (to blame, to criticize). It properly designates the action of reproaching someone for something. The form μομφή is an older poetic variant of the word μέμψις (which also means blame or complaint in classical Greek).
G3437.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:13. Paul uses it to exhort the Christians in Colossae to patience and mutual forgiveness. He acknowledges that brothers and sisters in Christ may have legitimate grievances against one another — it is a human reality. But instead of nurturing these complaints and using them as a reason to remain angry, believers are called to forgive one another "just as Christ" forgave them. The context emphasizes that forgiveness takes precedence over the claim for justice.
G3437.portee: This passage teaches us that even in a Christian community, frictions and grievances occur. What matters is our response: to harbor resentment or to choose forgiveness? Paul urges us to imitate the radical and unconditional forgiveness of Christ. Recognizing that you have a complaint against someone is an honest starting point — but it is also the moment when you must decide to let go and reconcile.

sens: A place where one lives, a house or accommodation
A place of rest or permanent stay
The action of living, staying long in one place
In a spiritual sense, the presence of God that establishes itself in a person's heart
G3438.detail:
1. A dwelling is properly a inhabited place, a house or accommodation (John 14:2: "In my Father's house are many dwelling places"). This word means a constructed place where one can reside, where one has their place.
2. The word also evokes the idea of staying, of residing durably somewhere — not just passing through, but settling in (John 14:23: "we will make our dwelling with him"). It is a rest, a stability.
3. Spiritually, Jesus promises that the Father and he will make their dwelling with the one who loves and obeys — that is, they will inhabit his heart, establishing a living and lasting presence there.
G3438.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb μένω (menō), "to stay, to dwell." Monē primarily denotes the action of staying or the place where one stays for a long time. It is a simple and natural word: the basic image is that of someone who settles in, who does not leave. In the Greek Old Testament, it is found to express the idea of residence and habitation.
G3438.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in John, chapter 14. In both verses, Jesus speaks of dwelling: first, the dwellings that the Father prepares in heaven (John 14:2), then the dwelling of the Father and the Son in the heart of the disciple (John 14:23). The meaning remains constant: a place of stable and personal presence. It is a comforting term, emphasizing not judgment or punishment, but welcome, a reserved place, communion.
G3438.portee: This word reveals the generosity of the Father: he prepares not just one place, but many dwellings, so that everyone has their place. It also shows that faith in Jesus is not an abstract doctrine, but a living relationship: when one loves Jesus and keeps his word, God comes to dwell in us. It is the promise of a real, intimate, and lasting presence — a comfort for the Christian who knows they are loved and awaited.

sens: Who is alone of its kind, without brother or sister
Who is one and only, incomparable, without equivalent
G3439.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a child who is alone: no brothers or sisters. The widow of Nain has lost her "only" son (Luke 7:12), and Jairus's daughter is his "only" daughter (Luke 8:42). It is a single child in the family, which makes their death particularly tragic for the dependent parents.

2. The word then shifts to the meaning of "unequaled, incomparable." When John speaks of the "only Son" of the Father (John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16), he is not just saying he is the only son of God — which would be true — but also that he is unequaled, incomparable in his relationship to the Father and in his glory. Abraham offers his "only" son (Hebrews 11:17): the one who concentrates all the promise and paternal love. The word then carries the idea of absolute preciousness and uniqueness.
G3439.origine: The word comes from the Greek "monos" (alone) and "genos" (race, species, descent). Literally, it is one who is "alone of its kind." In Hebrew, the corresponding term is "yahid" (יָחִיד), which also means "unique, alone, isolated." This Hebrew word already appears in the Old Testament in the Psalms to express isolation or uniqueness. The starting image is that of solitude in the family: the only child has no siblings.
G3439.emploi: The word "monogenēs" appears nine times in the New Testament, notably in Luke and John. Luke uses it three times for human children: the only son of the widow (Luke 7:12), the only daughter of Jairus (Luke 8:42), the only son of the father in the crowd (Luke 9:38). These three accounts highlight the tenderness and drama related to the loss of the only child. John applies it to Christ six times (John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16, 3:18, 1 John 4:9, Hebrews 11:17). In John, the word denotes the incomparable relationship of the Son to the Father: the "only" Son is the one who comes "from the Father" and reveals his heart. In Hebrews 11:17, Abraham offers his "only" son — Isaac — which emphasizes the gravity of the sacrifice and the absolute trust of faith.
G3439.portee: This word helps the Christian grasp the greatness of what God has done: he gave his Son, unique and incomparable, for the salvation of the world (John 3:16). The "uniqueness" of Christ is not a cold fact, but the expression of his unprecedented love and the infinite value of this sacrifice. For the believer, meditating on the "only" Son strengthens the confidence that God loves them as much as his only Father loves him.

sens: Indicates a restriction, a limitation: one single element, nothing more
Expresses an exception or a concession: all this, but also this
Marks a gradation: at minimum, at least
G3440.detail:
1. The word means that only one thing is at stake, that there is nothing more to add. Thus in Matthew 10:42, giving "only" a cold cup of water means that this gift, however modest, is sufficient: it is this single gesture that counts for the heavenly reward. The adverb focuses attention on a unique action or reality.

2. The word can also express that in addition to a first thing, there is a second: not only one, but also the other. In Philippians 1:29, Paul writes that the grace of God consists "not only" in believing in Christ, "but also" in suffering for him — there are two elements, and the second adds to the first. It is a progression.

3. The word can finally indicate a minimum or a minimal condition: at least this, at the very least that. It marks what must be retained or considered essential.
G3440.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "monos" (alone, unique) and directly relates to the idea of uniqueness and isolation. In Hebrew, the corresponding word in the Greek Old Testament is "lebad" (apart, alone), which also expresses this notion of isolation or singularity. The adverbial form "monon" transforms this adjective into a grammatical tool to modify and nuance the proposition: it speaks of what is unique or exclusive in a situation.
G3440.emploi: The adverb "monon" ("only") is very frequent in the New Testament. It is used in two main ways: first as a simple restriction marking the limitation to a single element ("only a cup of water"), and then in the formulas "not only... but also" to express a progression or addition of two elements. In Matthew 10:42, it is a restriction — the cup of water alone is sufficient. In Philippians 1:29, it is a formula of progression — not only to believe, but also to suffer. The context determines the usage.
G3440.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and rewards even modest and humble gestures, provided they are done with love. It also exhorts the reader not to think that a single virtue is sufficient for the Christian life: faith alone is not enough; one must also accept suffering and perseverance. Knowing this word helps to read the Bible accurately and to grasp how it nuances the life of a disciple.

sens: Who is without company, isolated, unique
G3441.detail:
1. Alone primarily means that a person is without company, isolated from others. Jesus "went up on the mountain to pray alone" (Matthew 14:23): he was physically separated from his disciples. This is a solitude of place or moment.

2. The word also designates what is unique, unparalleled. God alone is God: "To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God" (1 Timothy 1:17). Nothing and no one is added to Him; He is separate, incomparable.

3. Alone can also mean "exclusively," "only." Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God (Matthew 4:4): bread is not sufficient by itself. This usage marks a limit or restriction.

4. Finally, the word carries the idea of "abandoned" or "deprived of." A church that receives a message alone (without confirmations) feels helpless (Acts 18:25). This is a form of weakness or incompleteness.
G3441.origine: The Greek word monos comes from an ancient root meaning "one only" or "one." It is a very common adjective, which can also be used as an adverb when it modifies a verb or an adjective. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it generally translates levad (לְבַד), which carries the same idea of isolation or uniqueness. The same root has given rise in French to words like "monastery" (house of monks, who live alone) or "monologue."
G3441.emploi: Monos appears 111 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its uses can be divided into two main groups. First, as an adjective: it qualifies a person alone, Jesus withdrawing to pray, or a disciple isolated from others; it also qualifies God as the only master or only creator, emphasizing His absolute uniqueness (John 17:3, 1 Timothy 1:17). Secondly, as an adverb: alone modifies a verb ("believing alone is not enough"), an adjective ("only bread"), or combines with not to say "not only... but also" (Romans 5:3, Acts 19:26). This construction not only... but means that something is added to what has just been said.
G3441.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus experienced solitude — solitude of prayer, solitude of mission, and ultimately the solitude of the cross ("I am not alone; the Father is with me," John 16:32). It invites us to see that God alone deserves our sole trust and exclusive allegiance. For the believer, "alone" also means that no earthly force, no law, no human wisdom is sufficient; we must be attached to Christ and His word.

sens: Having one eye, being deprived of one eye
Figuratively, entering into divine life with a reduced but saved vision, rather than losing all access to the kingdom with an intact vision
G3442.detail:
1. The word literally describes the physical state of a person or creature who has only one eye: they are one-eyed. It is a simple anatomical observation.

2. Jesus uses this image to teach a major spiritual principle: it is better to accept a loss, a mutilation, a limitation of oneself, if it is the price of access to the kingdom of God, rather than to maintain the integrity of one's body and be lost for eternity. The disciple who "tears out his eye" — that is, who renounces what leads him to sin — enters into life "having only one eye" (Matthew 18:9), deprived of a part of himself, but alive. It is better than being thrown whole into hell. The image is deliberately shocking to awaken the conscience.
G3442.origine: The Greek word μονόφθαλμος (monophthalmos) is composed of μόνος (monos), "one only," and ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmos), "eye." It is a simple descriptive adjective, without particular etymological charge: it simply designates the physical condition of having one eye. Greek often borrows these compound words to describe bodily traits.
G3442.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same saying of Jesus, reported by Matthew (18:9) and Mark (9:47). It occurs in the context of scandal and temptation to sin: Jesus warns His disciples that if one of their members — here the eye, a symbol of desire and covetousness — leads them to sin, it is better to deprive themselves of it than to lose their soul. The use remains metaphorical and moral, not literal: Jesus does not prescribe self-mutilation, but uses this absurd and extreme image to clarify the hierarchy of values. Eternal salvation takes precedence over the integrity of the body.
G3442.portee: This word reminds the believer that the price of salvation can be costly and require real renunciations. It invites him to examine what in his life — his desires, habits, friendships — diverts him from God, and to be ready to renounce it. The implicit promise is that this apparent loss is actually an infinite gain: entering into eternal life is infinitely better than retaining one's carnal desires and being lost.

sens: Abandon someone in solitude
Be deprived of support or company
Remain without help in the face of life
G3443.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of leaving someone alone, abandoning them to their fate. It conveys the idea of rupture: one who was surrounded finds themselves isolated, without presence or support.
2. By extension, it describes the state of one who is deprived — who has lost their natural support. In 1 Timothy 5:5, the widow "who has remained in isolation" is one whose husband has died, who no longer has a protector and must face life alone.
3. It is also a spiritual condition: being alone in the face of circumstances, without human recourse. The abandoned widow must place all her hope in God.
G3443.origine: The verb comes from the adjective μόνος (monos), which means "alone, unique." The prefix -ō makes it a verb: "to make alone." The root evokes the idea of isolation, absence of company. The formation of the word follows the usual Greek logic: starting from a quality (alone) to create an action (leave alone).
G3443.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:5. Paul speaks of the widow who has remained alone, without a husband or other family supports. It is a technical term to designate the difficult condition of a widow in Paul's time — she loses both her legal protector and her source of livelihood. The context shows that the Church must assist these widows who have no one else: they are the most vulnerable, those who can only rely on God and the charity of believers.
G3443.portee: This word reminds us that abandonment, solitude, and loss of human support are never the final word for the believer. The widow who has no one can place all her hope in God — which Paul emphasizes by saying that she "continues in supplications night and day." The word also invites the Church not to leave the weakest in destitution: assisting the isolated widow is a sign of the Kingdom.

sens: The outward appearance of a person or thing, its visible silhouette
The deep essence of a being, what truly defines it and makes it what it is
G3444.detail:
1. The form is primarily what is seen: the silhouette, the concrete appearance. In Mark 16:12, the resurrected Jesus appears to the disciples "in another form" — his outward aspect has changed, they do not recognize him at first, even though it is truly him. It is the visible envelope.
2. But the word also designates the very essence, what deeply constitutes the being. In Philippians 2:6, Paul says that Christ "existed in the form of God": this is not merely about his appearance, but about his true divine nature. And in Philippians 2:7, by "taking the form of a servant", Jesus truly assumes human condition, not just the appearance. The form here is what one is, not just what one appears to be.
G3444.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to shape", "to mold". It designates the shape given to something, its characteristic structure. Greek philosophers used it to speak of the true essence of things, as opposed to their mere outward appearance. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words designating the visible form (like תַּבְנִית, tabnit, "what is constructed, shaped"), but also the splendor or glory (זִיו, zîv).
G3444.emploi: The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament. In Mark 16:12, it describes the change in appearance of the resurrected Christ — a visible change that even prevents the disciples from recognizing him immediately. The two uses in Philippians 2:6-7 are theologically decisive: they affirm that Jesus truly possessed the form (the nature) of God before the incarnation, and that he truly took on the form of a servant by becoming man. The term emphasizes the reality of what he is, beyond appearances.
G3444.portee: This word reminds us that the incarnation of Christ is not a mere disguise or deceptive appearance: he truly became man, he genuinely took on our condition. But it also affirms that before that, he truly possessed the divine nature. The "form" speaks of both what is seen and what one is; for Jesus, appearance and essence coincide.

sens: To give shape to something, to mold it
To take shape, to develop gradually
To be born and grow into being, to establish oneself durably
G3445.detail:
1. To give shape to something, to mold it — this is the basic image: that of shaping, like an artisan who forms a statue (Isaiah 44:13 speaks of the carpenter who shapes the wood). In Galatians 4:19, Paul uses this verb in a figurative sense: the formation of Christ in his disciples, as if Christ were gradually taking shape and life in them.

2. To take shape, to develop gradually — the verb can also mean the process by which something develops, grows, and takes its definitive structure. It is this development that Paul evokes when he speaks of Christ formed in his children in faith: it is a work that is accomplished little by little, like the gestation of a child.

3. To be born and grow durably — in theological language, "to form Christ" in someone means to allow the living Christ to establish and settle durably in the believer's heart, shaping their character, choices, and entire life.
G3445.origine: The verb comes from the Greek noun morphé ("form", "appearance"). It is the same root found in French in "morphology" (the study of form) or "transform". The starting image is that of shaping: giving a form to a material, molding it as one would with clay. This Greek verb often translates in the Greek Old Testament Hebrew verbs concerning creation or shaping.
G3445.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible in this precise sense: Galatians 4:19. Paul addresses his converts in Galatia and uses a maternal image ("the pains of childbirth") to express his ardent desire for Christ to be formed in them. This formation of Christ in his disciples is not a mere intellectual knowledge, but a profound transformation of being. It is a continuous process (the verb in the present suggests this), resembling a spiritual gestation. The formation of Christ in us is the work of the Holy Spirit and also requires our collaboration in faith.
G3445.portee: This word reveals that becoming a Christian is not a unique moment, but a living process: allowing Christ to be formed gradually in us. This means that our life of faith must correspond to the person of Christ, that his character must shape ours. It is an invitation to commitment and inner transformation, not to mere profession of faith.

sens: the external aspect, the visible form of a thing
a superficial resemblance, an imitation or semblance
the configuration or expression of an idea made visible
G3446.detail:
1. The word designates the form or aspect that is seen from the outside — what is shown to the eyes. In Romans 2:20, Paul speaks of "the standard of knowledge": it is the orderly exposition, the visible structure of the knowledge contained in the law, as it is taught and seen practiced.

2. By extension, the word can designate a deceptive appearance: in 2 Timothy 3:5, Paul denounces those who have "the appearance of godliness" but deny its power — they resemble the bark without having the heart. It is a semblance that lacks real substance.

3. Unlike the simple outer form (morphé), the word "morphôsis" emphasizes the concrete expression, the visible organization of a reality: what manifests, shapes, structures to be perceived.
G3446.origine: The word comes from the verb morphóô (to shape, to form) and the root morphé (form). It is the action or result of formation — not the raw form, but the form that has been constituted, that has been set in place. In Greek, morphôsis emphasizes more the process of formation or the formed state than the form itself (morphé). The word is rare and literary.
G3446.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 2:20, it describes the orderly structure of the Law as a standard of knowledge and truth. In 2 Timothy 3:5, it stigmatizes an outward appearance of godliness devoid of transformative power. In these two uses, morphôsis contrasts with the deep reality: on one side, a clear exposition of the true; on the other, a hollow semblance. The word always emphasizes what manifests, expresses, or shows, as opposed to what remains hidden or what acts truly.
G3446.portee: This word teaches the reader vigilance: a beautiful outward form, a well-ordered or pious appearance does not guarantee inner reality. True godliness, true knowledge, requires a cohesion between appearance and transformative power, between visible structure and the force of the Holy Spirit. This invites the believer to look beyond seductive exteriors, to seek the living substance.

sens: shape a calf statue
create a calf idol for worship
G3447.detail:
1. The verb refers to the concrete action of making, shaping a calf as a material object — here an idol. This is what the Israelites did at Sinai by melting down the gold from their ornaments (Acts 7:41).
2. Figuratively, it involves creating an object of worship intended to replace the true God. The calf becomes a symbol of false religion, a diversion from faith.
G3447.origine: The word is composed of ancient Greek: μόσχος (moschos, "calf, young bull") + ποιέω (poieō, "to make, create"). It is a verb formed to precisely describe the act of making a calf-idol. The word appears in the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) to translate the episode of the golden calf in Exodus 32.
G3447.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:41, in Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin. Stephen reminds the Jewish leaders of their ancestors' unfaithfulness at Sinai when they "made a calf" and worshiped it instead of waiting for Moses and the Law of God. This is a key moment in the narrative: it shows how Israel abandoned its God for a man-made object, even though this people had received direct revelation from the Lord.
G3447.portee: This word teaches us the danger of religious diversion: creating or worshiping an image in place of God is a constant temptation, even for those who have witnessed the greatest miracles. For us today, it is a call to examine our hidden idols — everything we mentally or spiritually create and to which we give the place that belongs to God alone.

sens: young bovine animal, male or female
animal sacrificed or offered in a feast
symbolic creature in a vision
G3448.detail:
1. The calf is a young bovine, male or female, raised primarily for its meat. In the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:23, 27, 30), the father joyfully welcomes his son back by killing "the fattened calf" — a fattened animal, thus of value, symbolizing celebration and abundance.
2. The calf plays an important role in the sacrifices of the Old Testament. At the ratification of the covenant at Sinai (Hebrews 9:19), Moses uses the blood of calves mixed with water to sprinkle the people and seal the pact with God. Later, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews reminds us that the ancient sacrifices — blood of goats and calves — could not provide true redemption, unlike the unique sacrifice of Christ (Hebrews 9:12).
3. In the vision of heaven in Revelation 4:7, the second of the four living creatures around the throne of God has the appearance of a calf, likely representing divine strength and power.
G3448.origine: The Greek word *moschos* primarily means a young shoot or sprout, then "descendant" or "young of an animal." It regularly translates the Hebrew *par* (bull) and *egel* (calf). The root evokes the idea of germination, growth — a calf is literally what is born and grows from the herd.
G3448.emploi: The word *moschos* appears six times in the New Testament, notably in the three passages of the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15) where the father, in his joy at finding his lost son, orders that a fattened calf be killed to celebrate. Two occurrences are found in Hebrews 9, in a theological reflection on the sacrifices of the Old Covenant: the blood of the calf is among the ritual elements that Christ replaced with his own blood. A final occurrence in Revelation 4 uses it symbolically to describe a heavenly creature. The word remains attached to the concrete context of the animal and its value, whether festive or sacrificial.
G3448.portee: For the reader, the calf of the prodigal son is the tangible sign of divine mercy: God does not merely forgive; he celebrates the repentant as someone precious. In Hebrews, the calf becomes a silent witness of transcendence: the ancient sacrifices, however sacred they may be, were only a shadow of Christ's definitive and perfect sacrifice. This word reminds us that God's grace is manifested not in abstract thoughts but in visible and generous acts.

sens: Fatigue and physical effort in work
Suffering and distress resulting from difficult conditions
Labor accomplished despite obstacles
G3449.detail:
1. Pain primarily refers to strenuous work, labor that costs a lot of energy and sweat. It is the daily physical effort, like that of Paul who "day and night at work" preaches the Gospel while working with his hands (1 Thessalonians 2:9).
2. It also describes the suffering and distress caused by the harsh conditions of life. Paul lists his pains: "exposed to many sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, frequent fasts, cold and nakedness" (2 Corinthians 11:27). These are not just efforts, but deprivations that exhaust both body and heart.
3. More broadly, pain is the persevering labor despite all obstacles — it is the image of the worker who does not give up, who continues "night and day" (2 Thessalonians 3:8), even when everything makes the task difficult.
G3449.origine: The Greek word mochthos comes from an ancient root (which already appears in Homer in the form mogos) evoking painful effort, the breathlessness of work. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like telaa (fatigue, weariness) and amal (work, pain), particularly in the Psalms and among the prophets to describe the labor of men or the suffering of the righteous.
G3449.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul's epistles (2 Corinthians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians). Each time, Paul uses it to describe his own apostolic ministry: the manual labor he performs to avoid being a burden to the churches, and the sufferings that accompany this life of service to Christ. The apostle does not complain about the pain — he presents it as inseparable from his calling to proclaim the Gospel. The word emphasizes both the physical intensity (hunger, cold, sleeplessness) and perseverance ("night and day").
G3449.portee: This word invites the Christian to see in pain — difficult work, physical trials — not a curse, but a possible sign of faithfulness to God's call. Paul does not complain; he recalls his self-denial to prove his sincerity. Pain thus becomes a testimony: it can be endured with dignity when it serves a cause greater than oneself.

sens: One who practices the musical art, who plays a musical instrument
Artist skilled in the arts, particularly music
G3451.detail:
1. A musician is a person capable of playing music and instruments. They are a craftsman of the musical art, someone who masters this art. In Revelation 18:22, the word refers to the instrumentalists who were part of the prosperous and joyful life of Babylon: "the sound of harpists, musicians, flute players, and trumpeters will never be heard in you again." The disappearance of musicians symbolizes the end of all cultural and festive life in the city.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to one who is an expert in music or the arts, capable of creating and performing. They are skilled, trained, and have developed their art.
G3451.origine: The Greek word « mousikos » comes from « mousa », which means « the Muse » — the inspiring deity of the arts and poetry in Greek mythology. Etymologically, it designates one who is inspired by the Muse, who practices an art. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew « zamar » (זְמָר), which means « to sing », « to make music ». The word belongs to the family of terms related to art and musical creation.
G3451.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:22. John lists the sounds and activities that will disappear at the fall of Babylon: musicians, players of various instruments (harp, flute, trumpet), as well as craftsmen of all trades and the sound of the millstone. The musicians symbolize here the elegance, culture, and joy of life of a prosperous city. Their absence marks complete silence, death, and desolation that will follow divine judgment.
G3451.portee: This word reminds us that music was an important element of worship and festive life in the Bible. In Revelation, the disappearance of musicians reveals a grave truth: all prosperity based on pride and idolatry is fragile and fleeting. It entirely depends on God's mercy and disappears when judgment comes. For the believer, this invites us not to place our trust in earthly riches, but to seek first the Kingdom of God.

sens: White and fatty substance that fills the interior of bones
Figuratively, what is deepest and most vital in a person
G3452.detail:
1. Marrow is the soft, white substance found at the core of bones. It is an image of the deepest, most hidden part: in Hebrews 4:12, the word of God penetrates "to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow," meaning it reaches the most intimate levels of our being, where we can no longer hide.
2. The word thus evokes what is vital and living deep within us. The word of God, sharper than a two-edged sword, goes so far as to separate and judge what is most secret in the heart, revealing our true thoughts and hidden feelings.
G3452.origine: The Greek word μυελός (marrow) literally designates the substance found inside bones. Its basic image is that of a deep substance, hidden at the heart of a structure: this is why it is used figuratively to denote what is deepest and most essential. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew מֹחַ (moach), which has the same literal and figurative meaning.
G3452.emploi: The word μυελός appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12. In this verse, the author describes the power of the word of God: it is so penetrating and sharp that it reaches the most hidden depths of our being, even to the marrow of the bones. It is a poetic way of saying that nothing can escape God's judgment, that our most secret thoughts and feelings are laid bare before Him.
G3452.portee: This word reminds us that we cannot hide from the word of God. It does not act only on the surface, on our visible words or actions, but penetrates to the heart of who we are, to our motivations and our most secret thoughts. This is both humbling and liberating: humbling, because nothing escapes us; liberating, because this word that penetrates us purifies and heals us from within.

sens: To be initiated into a secret, a mystery
To acquire hidden or reserved knowledge
To learn progressively, through experience
G3453.detail: 1. The word evokes initiation into a religious mystery — as in ancient Greek cults where certain secrets were reserved for those who had undergone an initiation ritual. It is "to learn" in the sense of "to be introduced to the secret of." 2. It also describes the acquisition of knowledge that is not easily obtained, requiring a kind of revelation or special instruction. 3. In Philippians 4:12, Paul uses it to say that he has learned to adapt to any situation — wealth or poverty, fullness or hunger — as if it were a secret entrusted to him, a wisdom acquired progressively through experience and practice in the Christian life.
G3453.origine: The word comes from a Greek root μύ- which means "to close the mouth" — the image is that of silence, mystery, that which remains hidden except for the initiated. The "mysteries" (μυστήρια) were in the Greek world the secret rites of worship. Here the word primarily means "to initiate someone by entrusting a secret to them," and then more broadly "to teach, to learn."
G3453.emploi: The word appears only once in the French Bible (Philippians 4:12). Paul uses it in the passive voice: "I have learned the secret." This is not about a pagan religious initiation, but about learning a spiritual attitude — having learned, through his apostolic experience, to remain at peace in abundance as well as in lack. It is a secret acquired not through a unique revelation, but through practice and teaching received from Christ.
G3453.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is not a theory, but a learning process: Paul did not "know" from the outset how to live detachment and trust; he had to learn it. This encourages the reader to see their own experience of difficulties and blessings, not as accidents, but as opportunities where God teaches them the wisdom and inner peace of the heart that knows its Lord.

sens: fictional story or imaginative invention, often clever or alluring
false narrative presented as true to deceive or mislead
set of beliefs or practices not based on truth
G3454.detail:
1. A fable is an invented story, forged by imagination. It is not a true account or a faithful testimony, but an elaborate fiction, sometimes crafted very skillfully: Peter speaks of "cleverly devised fables" (2 Peter 1:16), contrasting these deceptive stories with the true power of Christ that he witnessed with his own eyes.
2. More broadly, it refers to a false narrative presented to be believed, capable of leading someone away from the truth. This is why Timothy must "reject profane and silly myths" (1 Timothy 4:7) and refuse to cling to "Jewish fables" (Titus 1:14), which divert from true teachings.
3. The word also designates the error itself or what misleads: fables "turn away the ear from the truth" (2 Timothy 4:4), they captivate the mind and divert it from the true.
G3454.origine: The Greek word muthos comes from a root meaning "word" or "saying," but it has specialized to denote not just any discourse, but story, narrative — particularly fabulous or mythological stories. This is why in classical Greek thought, muthos stands in opposition to logos (the true narrative, reason): one is invention, the other truth. The letters of the New Testament take up this opposition to warn against "fables" that stray from authentic Christian teaching.
G3454.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the pastoral epistles and in Peter, with the meaning of deceptive fiction or false teaching. Timothy is warned against "fables and endless genealogies" (1 Timothy 1:4) and "profane and silly myths" (1 Timothy 4:7) — likely Jewish or Gnostic speculations circulating in the churches. Titus must also reject "Jewish fables" (Titus 1:14). Paul notes that people "will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths" (2 Timothy 4:4), showing how the seduction of fables leads away from the true gospel. Finally, Peter asserts that the teaching about Christ is not based on "cleverly devised fables" (2 Peter 1:16), but on the direct testimony of His majesty. Everywhere, fable stands opposed to apostolic truth and sound teaching.
G3454.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian faith rests on historical truth and testimony, not on inventions or speculations. It warns us against anything that would divert us from the clear teaching of Scripture — whether false doctrines, legends, or human imaginations — and calls us to seek the authenticity and solidity of the Gospel received from the apostles.

sens: To make the characteristic cry of an animal (ox, lion)
To shout with a loud and impressive voice
G3455.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the natural cry of animals: the bellowing of an ox or the roaring of a lion. It is an onomatopoeic word, imitating the sound itself. In Revelation 10:3, the mighty angel "cries with a loud voice, like a lion roars": the image of the roaring lion conveys the impressive power and authority of this cry.

2. By extension, it means to shout with a loud and imposing voice, one that fills with respect or fear. When someone "roars" like this, their cry is not ordinary: it carries power and majesty, like that of a mighty creature.
G3455.origine: The word comes from an onomatopoeic root that imitates the cry of cattle. In classical Greek, it appears mainly in poetry. The Greek Old Testament uses it notably to translate the cry of the animal in Job 6:5. The verb seeks to reproduce by sound the natural bellowing of the beast.
G3455.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 10:3. It is found in a solemn vision: the mighty angel descending from heaven lets out a cry like the roaring of a lion, and this cry immediately provokes the rumbling of the seven thunders. John chooses this rare and vivid word to mark the superhuman majesty of the moment and the thunderous impact of the angelic word on creation.
G3455.portee: This word invites the reader to feel the power and absolute authority of the divine word. The roaring of the angel symbolizes a proclamation that commands respect and fear, that resonates and demands obedience. For the believer, it is a reminder that the voice of God and His messengers is not gentle and quiet, but sovereign and irresistible.

sens: To turn up one's nose at someone or something, to express contempt
To mock, ridicule
To reject with disdain, to despise
To treat someone with derision
G3456.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the action of wrinkling the nose, a natural gesture of someone who pushes something away with contempt. It is the image of a grimace of disgust or disdain towards what is considered unworthy. In Galatians 6:7, Paul uses this word to say: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked," meaning that one cannot treat Him with disdain or despise Him with impunity.
2. More broadly, the word denotes the act of mocking someone, ridiculing them in words, turning them into a subject of derision. It is an expressed contempt, a mockery that humiliates. The underlying idea is that one considers the person or thing as unworthy of respect.
3. Figuratively, the verb can also mean to reject or despise something important, to treat it as negligible. When one mocks God, they refuse to acknowledge His power and justice, acting as if He has no importance or power.
G3456.origine: The word comes from the Greek noun "muktèr" which means "nose." The action of "muktèrizô" is therefore literally what the nose expresses: a wrinkling, a grimace. It is a verb formed from a part of the body to designate a gesture of natural and universal contempt. In Aramaic and Hebrew, words with similar roots (like "lâag" and "nâas") also express mockery and contempt, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses this verb to render them.
G3456.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament according to the provided usages, in Galatians 6:7 in the passive: "God is not mocked." Paul uses it to emphasize the impossibility of deceiving God or treating Him with disdain. It is a serious warning: anyone who thinks they can mock God and ignore the moral laws He has established deceives themselves. The context shows that one cannot sow evil with impunity and expect anything else: God sees all, and His justice will be executed.
G3456.portee: This verb reminds us that God does not tolerate insolence, contempt, or human pretension. To mock God is to forget His sovereignty and think that one can live without consequences by ignoring His will. Paul's warning invites the believer to reverence towards God and seriousness in their moral life: every act has consequences, visible or not.

sens: Belonging to a mill, part of a mill
Concerning the stones used to grind grain
G3457.detail:
1. The adjective "of millstone" describes something that belongs to a mill or is a part of it. In Luke 17:2, Jesus speaks of a "millstone" (a grinding stone), meaning a large stone intended to grind grain in a mill: it is a heavy and massive object.
2. The word emphasizes the function of the mill, which is to transform grain into flour by grinding between two stones. The millstone mentioned here is obviously enormous, as Jesus refers to it as a weight capable of sinking a man into the sea: it is an image of extreme weight, far heavier than an ordinary stone.
G3457.origine: The word comes from the Greek "mylos" (μύλη), which means mill. It is a derived adjective, formed to designate what belongs to or relates to the mill. The grain mill was a common installation in the ancient Mediterranean world: a structure with two circular stones, one fixed and the other rotating, that crushed the grain between them.
G3457.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:2. Jesus uses it to illustrate the terrible punishment reserved for anyone who causes a child or a small believer to stumble: it would be better for him to have a millstone tied around his neck and be thrown into the sea. The image is that of drowning under an exorbitant weight, expressing the horror of divine judgment in the face of the scandal of the innocent.
G3457.portee: This word from Jesus reveals the critical importance He places on protecting children and weak believers: anyone who leads them away from the path of God incurs a merciless judgment. It invites the reader to examine their own behavior towards those who are fragile in faith and reminds that responsibility towards the least is a matter of spiritual life or death.

sens: Circular stone used to grind grain
Grinding instrument in a mill
Weight or heavy object used as extreme punishment
G3458.detail:
1. The millstone is a large round and flat stone, used since antiquity to grind grain and make flour. It is a common tool of daily life: in Matthew 24:41, two women are working together at the millstone, showing that it was a common task. The sound of the millstone turning was familiar in every village, as recalled in Revelation 18:22 when it lists the sounds that will disappear from Babylon.
2. The millstone refers to the object itself, the instrument of the mill. In Revelation 18:22, we hear "the sound of the millstone" — it is the noise produced by the two stones turning against each other to crush the grain.
3. Jesus uses the millstone as an image of extreme punishment: it would be better for someone who causes a child to stumble "that a millstone were hung around his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42). The millstone here becomes a symbol of an overwhelming and deadly weight, the heaviest and most inescapable object one can imagine — certain drowning without return.
G3458.origine: The Greek word mulos simply refers to the millstone, the tool for grinding, a term attested in ancient Greek texts. It regularly translates the Hebrew word rehé, which has the same concrete meaning. The word expresses the idea of grinding, transforming hard grain into fine powder, hence its figurative use to describe irreversible destruction.
G3458.emploi: The word millstone appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in serious or significant contexts. Three occurrences (Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42, and another in Matthew 24:41) share the same type of usage: Jesus uses the millstone as an image of extreme weight. In Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42, it is an image of divine punishment — the same millstone that a woman operates every day becomes, hung around a man's neck, his instrument of death. In Matthew 24:41, the millstone is simply mentioned as the place where two women work, illustrating ordinary life interrupted by judgment. In Revelation 18:22, it is among the sounds of prosperous urban life that will disappear when Babylon is destroyed.
G3458.portee: The millstone in the Bible reminds us of the reality of divine judgment: the familiar, mundane object that everyone sees in daily use becomes the emblem of what is inevitable and without remission. Jesus uses this image to show the gravity of causing a child to stumble into sin — it is a crime of overwhelming weight. For the believer, it is a call to vigilance towards the little ones and an invitation to take seriously Jesus' words about the consequences of scandal.

sens: port city of Lycia in Asia Minor (modern Turkey)
G3460.detail: Myra is a coastal city in southwestern Asia Minor, in Lycia, where Paul and his companions arrive during their journey to Rome (Acts 27:5). It was an important port in the eastern Mediterranean, known particularly as a commercial transit point and a place for boarding ships.
G3460.origine: The name "Myra" designates a well-known ancient city. Its etymology is not certain in biblical or ancient secular sources, but it appears in the geographies of the Greek and Roman world as an established urban center.
G3460.emploi: Myra appears only once in the New Testament, during the account of Paul's journey to Rome to be judged before Caesar. Paul and his companions sail through Cilicia and Pamphylia before arriving at Myra, where they likely change ships to continue their journey (Acts 27:5). This mention illustrates the geographical and logistical reality of maritime travel in the first century.

sens: A number of ten thousand
A very large multitude, countless
A dense and pressing crowd
G3461.detail:
1. In the strict sense, a myriad refers to the number ten thousand — a precise figure in antiquity. In Acts 19:19, the books of magic burned are estimated at fifty thousand pieces of silver: that is fifty times ten thousand, a calculation of enormous value for the time.
2. More often, the word simply expresses a multitude so great that it cannot be counted. In Revelation 5:11, John sees "myriads of myriads" — one can no longer count, one can only admire the impossibility of numbering this heavenly crowd around the throne. Similarly, in Acts 21:20, the thousands of Jewish believers illustrate a dizzying growth of the Church.
3. The word also suggests a compact, dense crowd that presses together. In Luke 12:1, the people gather "by the thousands, so much so that they trample one another": it is the image of a human mass so dense that it crushes under its own weight.
G3461.origine: The Greek word μυριάς comes from the adjective μυρίος, which means "ten thousand." This root refers to a limit of what the ancient mind could easily count. The Hebrew word רְבָבָה (rebaba) in the Old Testament, to which the Greek often corresponds, has the same meaning, and both languages use this number as a symbol of the incalculable. This is why "myriad" has shifted from the precise number to the sense of "immeasurable quantity."
G3461.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, especially in Revelation and Acts. Three uses retain the nuance of the precise number: Acts 19:19 (fifty thousand pieces of silver), Acts 21:20 (thousands of believers), Luke 12:1 (crowd by the thousands). But four other uses soar into celestial hyperbole: Hebrews 12:22, Jude 1:14, and Revelation 5:11 use "myriad" or "myriads" to describe angels and heavenly creatures, beings that no human can truly enumerate. Revelation 9:16 repeats the motif with the horses of the army of horsemen. The word thus travels from the quantifiable to the immeasurable, from the earthly to the heavenly.
G3461.portee: For the Christian reader, the word "myriad" reveals how the Bible thinks about divine realities: it renounces exact counting and allows itself to be overwhelmed by the abundance and power of God. When heaven is described in myriads of angels, it is to inspire wonder and worship, not mathematical curiosity. The word invites a shift from calculation to admiration, showing that the greatness of God exceeds all human enumeration.

sens: To anoint a body with oils or aromatic perfumes
To prepare a body for burial by applying ointments
G3462.detail:
1. To anoint means to apply fragrant oils or ointments to the skin or clothing. It is an act of honor, tenderness, or care. In Mark 14:8, a woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus' body: it is the same act of anointing, but rich in spiritual meaning.
2. To embalm is to anoint a corpse with aromatics to preserve it and prepare it for burial, according to Jewish custom. The woman in Mark 14:8 thus anticipates Jesus' burial by anointing him in advance — a preparation for his death, but also an act of love that honors him even before he dies.
G3462.origine: The word comes from the Greek name μύρον (myron), which means "ointment" or "aromatic perfume." It is a precious substance made from fragrant oils and resins, very costly and reserved for solemn occasions. The verb μυρίζω literally expresses the action of applying myron. This practice of anointing is ancient and common in the Mediterranean world and the Near East.
G3462.emploi: The verb μυρίζω appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 14:8. It refers to the act of the woman who pours pure, very costly nard on Jesus' body a few days before his Passion. Jesus sees it as a prophetic action: she anoints him in advance for his burial, an act of love and faith in the face of his imminent death. This act, although criticized by the disciples for its apparent cost, is for Jesus an expression of devotion and will be remembered wherever the Gospel is preached.
G3462.portee: This word reminds us that love for Jesus is expressed through concrete and costly gestures, without calculation. The anointing by the woman teaches the reader that giving what one possesses most precious to Jesus — one's time, resources, heart — is more important than the reproaches of others or economic reasoning. It is an act of faith and tenderness that God does not despise.

sens: A very large and incalculable number
Exact figure of ten thousand units
G3463.detail:
1. The word first evokes a multitude so enormous that it seems almost limitless. When Paul says to the Corinthians, "even if you had ten thousand instructors in Christ," he is not counting precisely ten thousand people: he means that even if you had an incalculable number of instructors, you would still have only one spiritual father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Similarly, "ten thousand words in a tongue" simply means an inexhaustible flow of words (1 Corinthians 14:19).
2. The same word can also designate the precise number: ten thousand talents (that is, ten thousand times a thousand pieces of gold or silver), the astronomical sum owed by the servant in the parable of Matthew 18:24, impossible to repay in a human lifetime.
G3463.origine: This Greek word designates the number ten thousand, the highest number that the Greeks named directly (beyond that, they spoke of "multitudes of multitudes"). The image is of a crowd so numerous that it cannot be counted, hence its frequent use to simply mean "a huge quantity." The word has no direct equivalent in ancient Hebrew, where a single word was not used for this number.
G3463.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Matthew, it designates the concrete and colossal number of talents (18:24), an image of the insurmountable spiritual debt of the sinner. In Paul’s writings, in two passages of the same chapter (1 Corinthians 4:15 and 14:19), the word loses its numerical rigor: it becomes synonymous with "innumerable" or "excessive." This flexibility reflects common Greek usage, where ten thousand was both a real number and a symbol of infinity or absurdity.
G3463.portee: This word reminds the reader that the debts of sin are real and overwhelming, impossible to settle by our own strength — hence the grace of God in Jesus Christ. It also shows how the Bible speaks realistically about magnitudes: it does not hesitate to use enormous numbers to strike the imagination and demonstrate the extent of divine gift or judgment.

sens: Fragrant and precious substance used to anoint the body or honor it
Aromatic oil poured as a sign of respect or love
What expresses a mark of devotion or worship
G3464.detail:
1. Perfume is a costly substance, often contained in an alabaster jar, that was poured on the body to honor it. It is a rich and precious aromatic oil. The sinful woman in Luke 7:37 brings an alabaster jar full of perfume to pour on Jesus' feet.
2. Pouring perfume on someone was an act of honor, respect, and affection. It could accompany a supplication or express great esteem. In Luke 7:46, Jesus contrasts the absence of customary oil with the perfume that the woman poured on his feet.
3. Perfume also held religious and cultic significance: anointing someone with perfume was to consecrate them or manifest deep attachment. In John 12:3, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with perfume, an act of devotion before his death.
G3464.origine: The Greek word muron literally designates a fragrant oil or ointment. It comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to pour out," evoking the image of oil being poured. In the Greek Old Testament, muron primarily translates the Hebrew word shemen (oil), especially in the Psalms and Proverbs. It is an imported substance, costly and luxurious, reserved for solemn occasions or acts of great tenderness.
G3464.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, especially in the accounts of Jesus' anointing (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). It designates each time a precious aromatic oil poured on the body, particularly on the feet or head. In Matthew 26:7-12, the anointing at Bethany prophetically announces Jesus' burial. In Luke 7:37-46, the anointing by the sinful woman is an act of love and repentance. John 11:2 and 12:3 present Mary anointing Jesus as a sign of veneration. Revelation 18:13 mentions perfume among the goods of Babylonian commerce, highlighting its price and prestige.
G3464.portee: These anointing accounts reveal how faith is expressed through tangible acts of love towards Jesus. The costly perfume symbolizes the sacrifice of what one has most precious to honor the Lord. For the Christian, these passages teach that authentic worship does not count the cost, and that receiving Jesus is manifested through concrete and generous acts of devotion.

sens: Historical region in the northwest of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)
G3465.detail: 1. Mysia is a province of ancient Asia Minor, located in the northwest of this territory. It is a region that the Apostle Paul traverses during his second missionary journey reported in Acts. In Acts 16:7, Paul and his companions arrive "near Mysia" and consider entering Bithynia, a neighboring region, but the Spirit of Jesus prevents them. They then pass through Mysia and descend to Troas (Acts 16:8), a port city from which they will embark for Macedonia in Europe. This passage shows how God guides Paul's missionary movement by redirecting him to new territories.
G3465.origine: The name "Mysia" designates an ancient geographical region of Asia Minor, a well-known Roman province at the time of the New Testament. This historical territory has borne this name since classical antiquity.
G3465.emploi: The word "Mysia" appears only twice in the Bible, both in the account of Paul's journey in Acts 16:7-8. Paul and his companions pass through it on their way to Troas, guided by the Holy Spirit who prevents them from entering Bithynia. This episode illustrates how God providentially directs Paul's mission towards new regions, particularly towards Macedonia and thus towards Europe.
G3465.portee: This passage reveals that God actively directs the paths of missionaries, not only by blocking them (refusing Bithynia), but by redirecting them towards his will for the expansion of the Gospel. It teaches the reader that obstacles and detours in God's service can be signs of his direction, not failures.

sens: That which is known only to the initiated, a reserved secret
That which must not be revealed, what is kept hidden
A counsel or plan of God once hidden, now manifested in the Gospel
A particular truth of salvation, difficult to fully grasp
A secret design of God at work in history
G3466.detail:
1. The word first evokes a secret reserved for those who have been initiated: in the Greek world, "mysteries" were sacred rites and teachings that were revealed only to members of initiatory cults. In 1 Corinthians 4:1, Paul refers to the apostles as "stewards of the mysteries of God," meaning guardians of divine revelations.
2. More broadly, it refers to what is not disclosed, what must remain hidden. In 2 Thessalonians 2:7, Paul speaks of the "mystery of iniquity" that operates secretly, in the background.
3. In the New Testament, the word takes on a particular meaning: it designates the eternal plans and counsels of God, long veiled but now revealed by the Gospel. In Colossians 1:26, Paul describes the mystery as "hidden for ages and from generations, but now revealed to His saints."
4. Sometimes, the word denotes a particular truth of salvation: such as marriage as an image of Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:32), or the future fate of the dead in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:51). These truths remain profoundly mysterious even once revealed.
5. Finally, mystery can refer to God's secret plan at work in history: in Revelation 10:7, God's mystery must be fulfilled when the seventh trumpet sounds.
G3466.origine: The Greek word μυστήριον comes from the verb μυέω which means "to initiate" or "to be initiated." It primarily evokes the universe of mystery cults in the Greco-Roman world, where rites and teachings were secretly transmitted. The Greek Old Testament uses this word mainly to translate the Hebrew word רָז ("raz," secret or hidden counsel), particularly in the prophet Daniel. The word thus always retains this fundamental idea: something hidden, reserved, that must be discovered or received as a revelation.
G3466.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Pauline epistles and in Revelation. Paul uses it mainly to speak of the great mystery of salvation: God's plan in Jesus Christ, once hidden from the nations but now revealed to all. This mystery encompasses the incarnation of Christ (Ephesians 3:4), His love for the Church (Ephesians 5:32), and the gathering of Jews and Gentiles into one family (Ephesians 3:9). The word is also found in Mark and Luke in the expression "the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 13:11, Mark 4:11, Luke 8:10), where Jesus teaches through parables what only the Father reveals to His elect. Revelation uses the word to speak of heavenly realities veiled from human sight: the seven stars and the seven lampstands (Revelation 1:20).
G3466.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God acts with a plan, and that this plan, once secret, has become accessible to us through faith in Christ. It invites humility: even revealed, the mysteries of God remain deeper than our understanding. It also assures us that nothing escapes divine sovereignty, even what seems chaotic or incomprehensible. Finally, it emphasizes grace: we have received what was reserved, which could have remained hidden forever.

sens: to have the ability to distinguish distant objects
to perceive or understand what is far off or future
to enjoy spiritual clarity regarding God's promises
G3467.detail:
1. The word literally describes the ability to see things that are far away distinctly. It is the opposite of nearsightedness: a person who "sees afar" has good distance vision. In 2 Peter 1:9, the context contrasts the one who "sees afar" with the one who is "blind," unable to perceive beyond the present moment.

2. Figuratively, "to see afar" means to have insight, to understand the distant consequences of one's actions and the long-term stakes. It is to have a clear vision of one's spiritual destiny and the promises of God that extend beyond this life.

3. In 2 Peter 1:9, the Christian who forgets the purification of his former sins loses this spiritual clarity: he no longer "sees" afar, meaning he loses the living awareness of what Christ has accomplished for him and where his faith is leading him.
G3467.origine: The Greek word combines "myo" (to close the eyes, to blink) and "opsis" (sight, view). It literally designates one who closes their eyes to see, as one would do in front of a distant light source — hence "myopic," one who sees clearly only up close. Peter uses this same word, but positively: "to see afar" is to keep one's eyes open to the spiritual horizon, not to be blinded by the everyday.
G3467.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:9. The apostle uses it to describe the spiritual state of the believer who has forgotten to add to his faith the virtues listed in the preceding verses (virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, love). This Christian is spiritually myopic: he no longer "sees" afar, no longer clearly perceives his heavenly destination or the purifying work of Christ in him.
G3467.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to maintain a clear vision of his faith beyond immediate concerns. Forgetting where the purification received in Christ comes from leads to spiritual blindness, making one unable to "see afar" the beauty of his salvation and his present moral responsibility. It is a call to cultivate a living memory of the grace received.

sens: Injury or mark left by a blow, a violent impact
Minor wound caused by blows received, especially by whipping or flogging
G3468.detail:
1. A bruise is a visible injury on the skin, a mark or contusion caused by a blow or violent impact. It is a superficial but very real injury that testifies to the violence endured (Exodus 21:25 in the Greek Old Testament).
2. More specifically, the word designates injuries produced by whipping or flogging — these characteristic wounds that remain etched on the body. It is in this sense that the Bible speaks of Christ's bruises in 1 Peter 2:24: by the blows He endured, we have been spiritually healed.
G3468.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "blow, strike." It translates the Hebrew חַבּוּרָה (habburah), which precisely denotes the mark left by a blow. In ancient Greek texts, the word is used to describe visible injuries, contusions, and wounds from blows.
G3468.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Peter 2:24. The apostle Peter uses it to speak of the physical injuries that Jesus endured during His flogging before the cross. He refers to Isaiah 53:5, where the suffering servant is "bruised for our iniquities." This concrete term emphasizes the physical reality of Christ's suffering and establishes a link between His visible wounds and our spiritual healing.
G3468.portee: This word reminds the Christian that redemption is not an abstract doctrine: it cost Christ real, bodily, visible suffering. The Lord's bruises are not forgotten or minimized in the Christian faith — they are its foundation. This invites the believer to meditate on the price of his salvation and the tenderness of Christ who gave Himself for him.

sens: To find fault with something, to reproach it for a defect
To criticize, censure
To be a subject of reproach, disgrace
G3469.detail:
1. To blame is to express dissatisfaction towards someone or something by reproaching it for a defect, a fault, or reprehensible conduct. It is to judge negatively and make it known. In 2 Corinthians 8:20, Paul says he acts with care so that no one will blame him regarding the collection he administers: he wants his integrity to be above reproach.
2. To blame also means to openly criticize, to censure someone's conduct or work. It is to make a negative value judgment that can discredit. In 2 Corinthians 6:3, Paul states that the apostle gives no cause for scandal so that the ministry itself is not a subject of blame: his conduct must be blameless so that the Gospel is not tarnished.
3. The word can also refer to the state of the one who is blamed, the condition of one who has a bad reputation or is criticized — that is, to be a subject of reproach or disgrace.
G3469.origine: The Greek word μωμάομαι (blame) is formed from the root μῶμος (blame, reproach, defect), which evokes the idea of a visible stain or defect. It is a poetic and late verb, infrequent in classical Greek. The word expresses the action of pointing out a defect, as one would point out a stain on clothing. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this verb translates the Hebrew מאוּם (to blame, to criticize) in Proverbs 9:7.
G3469.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters to the Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 6:3, Paul uses it in the passive to say that the apostolic ministry must not become an occasion for reproach or scandal: it is a matter of credibility and testimony. In 2 Corinthians 8:20, Paul again uses the verb to affirm that he administers the collection with such care that no one will be able to blame him or suspect him of dishonesty. In both cases, blame is an affront to reputation, a criticism that could weaken the Christian ministry. Paul is aware that apostles must be blameless, not only in their actions but also in how others perceive them.
G3469.portee: This word teaches that the Christian life, especially that of God's servants, must be lived with particular vigilance regarding reputation and credibility. It is not about seeking perfection, but about avoiding giving legitimate reasons for reproach. Paul shows that moral integrity and prudence in managing resources or apostolic service are essential so that the Gospel is not discredited by human weaknesses. This reminds Christians that their conduct has consequences: it can strengthen or weaken their testimony.

sens: physical defect on the body
dishonor or moral reproach
moral stain or disgrace
a person marked by sin or vice
G3470.detail:
1. Literally, a stain or mark that disfigures the body — a visible imperfection. It is primarily a medical and physical term: in Leviticus, the Law forbids priests from presenting offerings or approaching the altar if they have a stain or physical defect (Leviticus 21:17).

2. Figuratively, a stain becomes a reproach, a shame, a dishonor — that which sullies reputation or character. This is why one can speak of a person "without stain" to describe someone impeccable: the Lamb of God, in the ultimate sacrifice, is presented as pure and without stain (1 Peter 1:19).

3. Applied to sin and immorality, the word designates the moral stain itself, the spiritual defect that marks a person and renders them unworthy. In 2 Peter 2:13, false teachers are described as "blemished and stained" (literally "stains"), because their carnal actions and deceptions morally defile them.
G3470.origine: The Greek word mōmos comes from an ancient root denoting a visible mark, a wound, or a deformity. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), it regularly translates the Hebrew word mûm, which means exactly the same thing: a physical defect rendering a person or offering unfit for service or sacrifice. The image always starts from the concrete — what is seen — to extend to the moral and spiritual realm.
G3470.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved New Testament: 2 Peter 2:13. But it fits into a well-established theology. The Old Testament uses it to describe physical defects that rendered one unfit for temple service. Biblical Greek extends it to moral and spiritual meaning: a person can be a "stain," a living blemish in the community, due to their immorality or false teachings. In 2 Peter, it is the false teachers who indulge shamelessly (already transposed to mean "to delight in") and act as deceivers: they themselves are marks of dishonor, stains in the body of the Church.
G3470.portee: This word reminds us that sin and immorality are not isolated acts: they mark, stain, and disfigure the one who commits them. In contrast, the image of Christ "without stain" shows the absolute purity of the sacrifice offered for us. The Christian who walks with Christ must aspire to this moral purity, aware that evil leaves traces; it is also a call to discern and reject false teachers who, far from sanctifying, stain the community.

sens: To become tasteless, to lose its taste or distinctive quality
To become foolish, unreasonable
To be rendered useless or ineffective
To make someone or something ineffective or ridiculous
G3471.detail:
1. The primary, very concrete meaning speaks of something that loses its flavor: salt that no longer seasons, that has become bland. This is the image in Matthew 5:13 and Luke 14:34: salt that has lost its nature, thus its usefulness. The verb denotes this process of degradation where something becomes unusable because it has lost what defined it.
2. Figuratively, it means to lose wisdom, to become foolish or unreasonable. Romans 1:22 uses it for the wise who, instead of recognizing God, "have become foolish": they have lost the judgment that honored them.
3. The word can also mean "to render ineffective," "to reduce to nothing": the wisdom of the world is "convicted of folly" in 1 Corinthians 1:20, that is, rendered absurd in the face of God's wisdom.
4. In this last usage, the meaning is more active: not only to lose, but to be made foolish, to be stripped of value or credibility.
G3471.origine: The verb comes from the adjective "μωρός" (moron), which means "foolish" or "stupid." The family of the word evokes the absence of discernment, foolishness. The verb adds the idea of becoming or being made so. In Hebrew, parallel passages from the Greek Old Testament use "בָּעַר" (bâ'ar, "to burn, consume") or "שָׂכַל" (sâkhal, "to act wisely") in the passive, which reinforces the idea of loss or transformation.
G3471.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in a context where something or someone loses its substance or effectiveness. Matthew and Luke apply it to salt that "loses its flavor": it is a concrete and vivid teaching about the disciples — if they cease to be the salt of the earth, they are of no use. Romans 1:22 describes the unbelievers who, instead of recognizing God, "have become foolish" — sin changes their clarity into blindness. In 1 Corinthians 1:20, Paul says that God "has made foolish the wisdom of the world": the verb expresses how the cross renders human boasting ridiculous. The word thus oscillates between a passive sense (to lose, to become) and a sense where God or the context renders something ineffective.
G3471.portee: This verb challenges the believer regarding their faithfulness. Just as salt must remain salty to be useful, the disciple must maintain their discernment and distinction to be effective in the world. It also reminds us that human wisdom, without God, is mere folly: this word frees the Christian from the fear of judgment from the wise of the age and invites them to seek true wisdom in Christ.

sens: Lack of good sense, absurdity in the eyes of reason
Absence of wisdom, erroneous judgment
What seems unreasonable or nonsensical to one who judges according to human logic
G3472.detail:
1. Foolishness is primarily the lack of good sense, what is absurd and contrary to reason. This is why the preaching of the cross, which tells of an innocent man being crucified to save the world, seems foolish to those who do not believe in Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:18, 1:23).
2. It is also the absence of wisdom, the false judgment of one who does not grasp the true nature of things. The natural man, guided only by his human intelligence, judges spiritual realities as foolishness because he does not have the Spirit of God to understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14).
3. More broadly, this word designates what seems unreasonable when measured against the wisdom of the world. Yet the wisdom of the world, however brilliant it may be, is itself foolishness before God, because it does not know Him (1 Corinthians 1:21, 3:19).
G3472.origine: The Greek word mōria comes from the adjective mōros, which means "foolish, lacking good sense." This root evokes the idea of someone who does not understand, who lacks discernment. The adjective mōros stands in contrast to sophos (wise): it is one who does not have wisdom. The word belongs to an ancient Greek family and expresses the fundamental contrast between true wisdom and the absence of good sense.
G3472.emploi: This word appears only in the First Letter to the Corinthians, exactly five times (1:18, 1:21, 1:23, 2:14, 3:19), all in the passage where Paul explains the central paradox of the Gospel. Paul plays on the contrast between what the world calls foolishness (the cross of Christ) and what God calls wisdom. The meaning remains constant: it is always the erroneous judgment of those who measure divine realities against the standard of human reason. More specifically, for the believer, the Gospel is not foolishness (it is the power of God); for the non-believer, it is (because he cannot understand it spiritually).
G3472.portee: This word reveals to the Christian reader that one should not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, even if it seems absurd in the eyes of the world. It reminds us that God's wisdom infinitely surpasses that of men, and that what seems unreasonable at first glance may be the greatest wisdom. Understanding this contrast frees the believer from the need to justify the Gospel according to worldly logic: he can adhere to it by faith, guided by the Spirit.

sens: stupid or absurd words
nonsensical conversation
babble that lacks seriousness and wisdom
G3473.detail:
1. The word designates stupid or absurd words, devoid of meaning or value. In Ephesians 5:4, Paul contrasts it with "thanksgiving": it refers to vain words that serve no good purpose, distracting and diverting from the seriousness of the Christian life.
2. It is also light babble, a discourse that lacks wisdom and depth, which does not respect the dignity of the speaker or those who listen. In the context of Ephesians, Paul invites believers to banish this type of futile conversation from their communal life.
G3473.origine: The word comes from the root "môros" (fool, foolish) and "logia" (word, discourse). It is the speech of the fool — not mental insanity, but the folly of one who speaks without thinking, without seriousness. The word is rare in the Bible: a single known occurrence in Ephesians 5:4.
G3473.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:4. Paul lists several categories of words to avoid among believers: "filthy" (or "shameful") talk, "foolish talk," and "crude joking." This is in the context of his exhortation to purity and honesty in the Christian life — a life oriented towards thanksgiving and praise to God, not towards hollow or hurtful amusements.
G3473.portee: This word reminds the Christian that his words reveal his heart and level of spiritual maturity. Speaking sensibly, with seriousness and kindness, is not rigidity: it is the fruit of a life filled with the Spirit of God. Christian joy is not futile amusement, but praise and thanksgiving.

sens: Lacking intelligence, discernment, wisdom
Acting without thinking, without prudence
Empty of good sense, devoid of judgment
What is absurd or contrary to reason in the eyes of the world
G3474.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a dull spirit, incapable of understanding clearly. Jesus calls one who insults his brother by saying "Raca!" (Matthew 5:22) a "fool": it is failing to see that one offends the dignity of his neighbor before God.
2. It is also the absence of prudence: the foolish virgins (Matthew 25:3) do not take oil for their lamps, even as the time for the wedding approaches — they act without foreseeing what will happen.
3. The man "foolish according to this age" (1 Corinthians 3:18) is one who thinks himself wise by following the logic of the world, but who understands nothing of true divine values.
4. Paradoxically, Paul calls the death of Christ on the cross "foolishness" (1 Corinthians 1:25), while it is in reality the very wisdom of God: what seems senseless to men is the fulfillment of divine will.
G3474.origine: The Greek word μωρός comes from a root expressing the idea of heaviness, slowness, absence of mental liveliness. In ancient Hebrew, it corresponds to נָבָל (naval), which describes a heart closed to the wisdom of God. Thus, it is a word that speaks less of malice than of blindness: biblical foolishness is an inability, whether willed or not, to grasp what truly matters.
