G3474.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew and Paul. Matthew uses it for Jesus' judgments: the angry man who insults, the virgins without reserve of oil, the Pharisees who do not see that the gold of the temple is sanctified by the temple itself (Matthew 23:17). Paul uses it more radically: he confronts the "foolishness" of the world — its sterile debates, its rejection of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:25, 1:27) — with the hidden wisdom of God. The "foolishness" that Paul calls to recognize is not a moral defect, but a blindness to divine realities. It stands in opposition to faith and the wisdom that comes from the Holy Spirit.
G3474.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine his own judgments: am I truly wise, or am I blinded by the logic of the world? It also calls for humility: the cross of Christ is "foolishness" in the eyes of men, and yet it is the heart of salvation. It is an invitation to revise our criteria of wisdom and to allow ourselves to be transformed by the Gospel rather than by the spirit of this age.

sens: Prophet and deliverer who led the people of Israel out of Egypt
Mediator of the old covenant, author of the Law
Symbol of the old divine economy, in contrast with Jesus
G3475.detail: 1. Moses is the great prophet and deliverer of Israel. The New Testament refers to him as the one through whom God gave the Law at Sinai and who led the people in the desert for forty years. He appears transfigured with Jesus on the mountain (Matthew 17:3), marking his central place in the history of salvation. 2. His name becomes inseparable from the Law he received: the expression "the law of Moses" constantly recurs to designate the entirety of the prescriptions given by God (Luke 2:22, Acts 15:5). Synagogues read "Moses" every Sabbath (Acts 15:21), showing that his authority reigns over the religious life of Judaism. 3. For the apostles, Moses prefigures Jesus: John 1:45 recalls that "Moses wrote in the law" about the one who was to come, and the Epistle to the Hebrews compares Jesus to Moses, showing that the former is a servant in the house while the latter is its son and master (Hebrews 3:2-5).
G3475.origine: The name Moses comes from the Hebrew Moshé (מֹשֶׁה), whose exact meaning remains debated: perhaps "drawn from the waters" (echoing his rescue from the Nile as a child) or "the one who draws out." It is an Egyptian name Hebraized. In the Hebrew Old Testament and in the Greek translation of the Septuagint, the same name designates the same man: the leader of Israel who received the Tablets of the Law and was the mediator of the covenant at Sinai.
G3475.emploi: Moses is named 79 times in the New Testament, more often than any other character from the Old Testament. He appears in the Gospels as a figure of legal authority and mediation: when the Pharisees ask for a divorce, they invoke "Moses" (Matthew 19:7), and the sick must perform the rites "that Moses prescribed" (Matthew 8:4). In Acts, Paul summarizes the entire Old Testament by mentioning "Moses and the prophets" (Acts 26:22), establishing a continuity. But a tension emerges: in John 1:17, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" while "the law was given through Moses," suggesting a surpassing. The Epistle to the Hebrews develops this idea, asserting that Moses was faithful "as a servant" while Jesus is faithful "as a son" (Hebrews 3:5-6), marking the transition from one economy to another.
G3475.portee: For the Christian reader, Moses embodies the old order of the Law: just, necessary, but destined to be surpassed. Understanding Moses is crucial to grasp how Jesus does not reject Scripture but perfects it: he does not come to abolish, but to fulfill. His role reminds us that God has always acted to save his people, and that the New Testament is not a break but the promised culmination from the beginning.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the line of Judah
G3476.detail: Nahshon is a figure from the Old Testament who appears in the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke. He is the son of Amminadab and the father of Salmon, holding an important place in the chain of ancestors of the Messiah.
G3476.origine: The Hebrew name נַחְשׁוֹן (Nahshôn) likely means "diviner" or is related to "serpent" (nahash). In the biblical genealogical lists, Nahshon is mentioned as early as the book of Numbers as the prince of the tribe of Judah.
G3476.emploi: Nahshon appears twice in the New Testament, in both genealogies of Jesus: first in Matthew (1:4), which traces from Joseph to the ancestors of David, and then in Luke (3:32), in the genealogy that goes back to Adam. These two occurrences testify that Jesus is from the royal line of Judah, establishing his legitimacy as the son of David. Although few details are given about his personal life, his inclusion in these genealogies shows his importance in the history of salvation.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G3477.detail: Naggai is a man who appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke. He is presented as the father of Amos and the son of Mattathias (Luke 3:25). This genealogy traces from Jesus back to Adam, showing the continuity of God's plan throughout history. Naggai represents an ordinary but necessary link in this long chain of ancestors that led to the birth of the Savior.
G3477.origine: The name Naggai is of Hebrew origin. It appears rarely in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its precise meaning is unknown to us. The fact that Luke includes him in his genealogy shows that he is an important historical figure for the transmission of God's people, even if the details of his life are not reported to us.
G3477.emploi: Naggai appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Luke 3:25, in the genealogy of Jesus. Luke places this man in a period prior to David, in the lineage traced by the evangelist from Adam to Jesus through Joseph. This passage shows how Luke emphasizes the continuity of sacred history through many generations, most of whom are completely unknown to us otherwise.

sens: City in Galilee, Israel, in northern Palestine
Place where Jesus grew up and spent his childhood
The term 'Nazarene' to refer to Jesus and his disciples
G3478.detail:
1. Nazareth is a city in Galilee, a region in northern Israel. It appears twelve times in the New Testament, always as a specific geographical location. It is where Mary lived before the Annunciation (Luke 1:26) and where Joseph and Mary settled after returning from Egypt (Luke 2:39).
2. Nazareth is the place where Jesus was raised and grew from childhood to adulthood. Luke reports that "according to his custom, he entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day" (Luke 4:16), showing his attachment to the religious life of this small town. It is from Nazareth that Jesus began his public ministry after his baptism.
3. The name of the city gave rise to the title "Nazarene" to refer to Jesus and his disciples. Matthew cites the prophet: "He will be called a Nazarene" (Matthew 2:23), establishing a link between the place of his childhood and his mission. This nickname constantly reminds of the humility of his earthly origins.
G3478.origine: The name Nazareth comes from a Semitic form (Hebrew or Aramaic) whose exact etymology is uncertain. Some scholars have seen a connection with the Hebrew word "netser" (shoot, branch), a messianic allusion to the prophet Isaiah speaking of a shoot that will come from Jesse. Others link it to "nazir" (consecrated, separated). However, these connections remain hypothetical: Nazareth is primarily the historical name of this small Galilean locality.
G3478.emploi: Nazareth appears in all four Gospels and in Acts (twelve occurrences in total). It plays a fundamental role in the narrative of Jesus' childhood: it is where the angel Gabriel announces to Mary that she will bear a son (Luke 1:26), and where Jesus spends his childhood and adolescence (Luke 2:4, 39, 51). At the beginning of his public ministry, Jesus returns to Nazareth to preach in the synagogue (Luke 4:16), a moment when his compatriots reject him. The city is not prestigious: Nathanael expresses doubt that "anything good" could come from "Nazareth" (John 1:46), showing the disdain that the Jews felt for this lost village. Jesus is regularly called "the prophet from Nazareth" (Matthew 21:11) or "the Nazarene," which shows that his geographical origins stuck with him, even after his extensive ministry in other regions.
G3478.portee: Nazareth reminds us that Jesus, the Son of God, lived an ordinary life in a small, unrenowned town. It is an invitation for every believer to recognize that God often acts through humble paths and obscure places. The disdain that Nazareth elicited from Jesus' contemporaries also speaks to the dignity given to what seems insignificant: God does not need a great city or a prestigious family to accomplish his work. This small town thus becomes a symbol of humility and trust in the hidden power of God.

sens: inhabitant of Nazareth
disciple or follower of Jesus
Jesus himself, identified by his origin
G3479.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone who comes from Nazareth, a small town in Galilee. It is a gentilice — a name based on the place of origin (as we would say "a Parisian"). The Gospels use it to remind that Jesus grew up there.
2. The term takes on a religious connotation: it becomes a nickname for the disciples or followers of Jesus — those who follow him and believe in him. In Acts 24:5, Paul is accused of being a leader of the Nazarenes, meaning a leader of Christians.
3. In the accounts of the Passion and resurrection (Mark and Luke), it is applied to Jesus himself for identification: "Jesus the Nazarene," says the demon in Mark 1:24, or the angel in Mark 16:6. It has become his distinctive title.
G3479.origine: The Greek word Nazarene comes from the Hebrew name Nazareth (נָצְרַת), whose exact etymology remains debated, but which designated a town in lower Galilee. The Greek form adds the ending -os to form an adjective of origin or belonging. In the Greek Old Testament, the same word translates Hebrew references related to this place or its inhabitants.
G3479.emploi: The word appears six times in the Gospels, exclusively in Mark and Luke, at key moments in the story of Jesus. In Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34, a demon or an unclean spirit cries out "Jesus the Nazarene" as Jesus enters the synagogue: it is an act of supernatural recognition or challenge. In Mark 10:47, Bartimaeus calls him this — a confession of faith. In Mark 14:67 and Luke 24:19, it is the title by which Jesus is designated or identified during the Passion and after the resurrection. The word only appears in these Gospels and reflects the tradition of Jesus being from Nazareth, even though Matthew and John prefer other expressions.
G3479.portee: The term "Nazarene" anchors Jesus in a concrete and humble story: he comes from a small town without prestige. It reminds the reader that the Son of God accepted an ordinary humanity and without apparent glory. For the early Church, it was also a sign of identity: to be Christian was primarily to follow "the one from Nazareth," a rabbi from Galilee who became Master and Lord.

sens: Inhabitant or native of the city of Nazareth in Galilee
Title given to Jesus because of his place of origin
G3480.detail:
1. A Nazarene is a person from Nazareth, a small town in Galilee. It is simply an adjective of origin, as one might say "a Parisian" or "a Lyonnais." The Bible mentions this town when it recounts that Jesus "came to dwell in a city called Nazareth" (Matthew 2:23).
2. The word particularly designates Jesus in the accounts of the New Testament. The apostles and the crowds call him "Jesus of Nazareth," which recalls where he came from and who he was. Peter says to the authorities: "It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, and whom God raised from the dead" (Acts 4:10). The demoniacs, the blind, the Roman soldiers all identify him by this title: "Jesus of Nazareth."
G3480.origine: The Greek word Nazōraios comes from the Hebrew name of the city: Nazareth. It simply designates the inhabitants of this place, formed according to the usual pattern of Greek ethnic adjectives (like Ioudaios for "Jew"). The city of Nazareth itself was a town of little importance, located in northern Galilee; this title remains humble, speaking of Jesus as a man from the province.
G3480.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the New Testament, almost entirely in the Gospels and Acts. Matthew 2:23 uses it to justify that Jesus settled in Nazareth and received this nickname. In the Gospels (Luke, John), the crowd and the blind call him this to identify him. In Acts, the apostles used this title in their public speeches: Peter uses it to preach (Acts 2:22, 4:10), Paul refers to it when speaking of his encounter with the risen Lord (Acts 22:8), and the opponents of the Church cite it to designate Christians as "the sect of the Nazarenes" (Acts 24:5, 26:9). Thus, it is a humble yet foundational title of Jesus' identity in apostolic preaching.
G3480.portee: This humble title reminds us that Jesus was rooted in concrete history: a man from a specific place, a region, a culture. He was not a mythical figure floating outside the world, but someone who could be encountered, who could be described by his origin. For the disciples and for us, this detail says that God incarnated himself in ordinary reality, the small town, daily life.

sens: Son of David in the genealogy of Jesus
G3481.detail: Nathan is a son of David mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke. He is part of the ancestral line that traces back from Jesus to David, between Melea (his father according to Luke's genealogy) and Mattatha (his own father according to this same list). This Nathan in the Lucan genealogy is distinct from the prophet Nathan of the Old Testament.
G3481.origine: The name Nathan comes from the Hebrew נָתַן (natan), which means "to give." It is a common theophoric name in ancient Israel, carrying the idea of what God gives. Several biblical characters bear this name, including the prophet Nathan who advised King David (2 Samuel 12).
G3481.emploi: Nathan appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:31. He is a link in the genealogy of Jesus, which Luke presents by tracing back from Jesus to Adam. This genealogy is distinct from that of Matthew and follows a different line of Davidic descent. Nathan the son of David is presented there as an ancestor of Jesus according to the flesh.

sens: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus
Disciple known for his integrity and absence of duplicity
Called by Jesus after being introduced by Philip
G3482.detail:
1. Nathanael is one of the twelve apostles, a companion of Jesus from Cana in Galilee. He appears in the Gospel of John during the calling of the first disciples (John 1:45-49) and is mentioned among the apostles gathered after the resurrection (John 21:2).
2. Jesus characterizes him as "truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit" (John 1:47), highlighting his moral integrity and absence of duplicity. This quality distinguishes him among the disciples.
3. Nathanael immediately recognizes Jesus as "the Son of God" and "the King of Israel" (John 1:49), which shows the clarity of his faith once he has met the Lord in person.
G3482.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew Nathanael, which means "God has given." It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, expressing gratitude towards the Lord. Most scholars identify Nathanael with Bartholomew, another apostle mentioned in the lists of the Twelve in the other Gospels.
G3482.emploi: Nathanael is named six times in the New Testament, exclusively in John. John presents him as an honest disciple, without malice, who expresses his trust in Jesus directly. Philip introduces him by announcing that the expected Messiah has come (John 1:45). Nathanael initially expresses skepticism — "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46) — but immediately abandons his prejudices when he meets Jesus himself. The last mention places him among the disciples gathered during a resurrected appearance in Galilee (John 21:2), confirming his importance in the apostolic group.
G3482.portee: The example of Nathanael encourages the reader to examine their own prejudices in light of a personal encounter with Jesus. His declaration of faith as soon as he meets the Lord invites a simple and courageous confession. His integrity recognized by Jesus also shows that God knows the heart of each person and honors those who walk without deceit.

sens: Simple affirmation in response to a question
Agreement or consent given
Solemn confirmation, oath
Assent to an assertion
Emphasis or intensity in the repeated affirmation
G3483.detail:
1. The word "yes" is the simplest particle of affirmation: it is used to respond positively to a question. When Jesus asks his disciples, "Do you believe that I can do this?" they respond, "Yes" (Matthew 9:28).
2. It expresses consent or personal commitment. The Canaanite woman says to Jesus, "Yes, Lord" while humbly accepting his teaching (Matthew 15:27); Peter responds, "Yes, Lord" when he affirms his love for Jesus (John 21:16).
3. It serves to solemnly affirm a truth or confirm what has just been said, often with religious or moral significance. Jesus says, "Yes, Father, I praise you that you have chosen this" confirming God's plan (Luke 10:21).
4. It marks assent to an assertion made by another, as when a witness says "Yes" to confirm the accusations against him (Acts 5:8).
5. When repeated twice ("Yes, yes"), the word gains strength and solemnity, opposing "No, no" to emphasize the importance of a promise or affirmation (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12).
G3483.origine: The Greek word ναί comes from a very ancient root of affirmation, and it is probably related to similar forms in Hebrew and other Semitic languages to say "yes." It is the direct opposite of the Greek οὔ ("no"). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew כֵּן ("yes, certainly"). It is a fundamental word for human and theological communication: saying "yes" or "no" engages the entire frankness and sincerity of the speaker.
G3483.emploi: The word "yes" appears about 30 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the Epistles. It primarily serves to respond to questions: disciples and crowds confirm their faith or understanding (Matthew 13:51). It also marks decisive moments: Peter confesses his love to Jesus (John 21:15-16), the Canaanite woman acknowledges the wisdom of the Master (Matthew 15:27). Paul uses it to affirm that his word is reliable, not contradictory (2 Corinthians 1:18-19). James and John emphasize the importance of keeping promises by simply saying "yes" without swearing (James 5:12; Revelation 1:7, 22:20). The double "yes, yes" reinforces the intensity of the commitment or affirmation.
G3483.portee: For the Christian reader, this small word reminds us of the importance of sincerity and transparency. Saying "yes" engages all our words and our faithfulness; that is why Jesus and James teach to simply say "yes" without swearing (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12). It also invites us to freely acknowledge God's authority and the beauty of His plan, as Jesus does by saying "Yes, Father" (Luke 10:21). It is a word of personal adherence: every "yes" we pronounce towards God is an act of faith and trust.

sens: Village in Galilee located in Israel
G3484.detail: Nain is a small village in Galilee, Israel. It is where Jesus raises the only son of a widow (Luke 7:11), an event that demonstrates His compassion and power over death.
G3484.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew נָאָה (naah), which means "pleasant" or "beautiful." It is a modest place in Galilee, the northern region of Israel where Jesus carried out a significant part of His ministry.
G3484.emploi: Nain appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 7:11. Matthew and Mark do not mention this village. It is the site of a particular miracle: Jesus encounters the funeral procession of a deceased young man and brings him back to life. This event showcases Jesus' tenderness towards the grieving and His authority over death itself.
G3484.portee: This account invites the reader to recognize that Jesus did not come merely to teach or heal: He also comes to comfort the brokenhearted and conquer death. The encounter at Nain reminds us that our Lord sees human distress and responds with power and mercy.

sens: sacred building where a deity is worshipped
the innermost chamber of the temple, the sanctuary reserved for the god
the temple of Jerusalem, center of Jewish worship
the body of believers as God's dwelling
the body of the resurrected Christ as God's temple
G3485.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a religious building where people come to pray and make sacrifices to a deity. This is the broadest sense: in Acts 17:24, Paul speaks of the temples where gods dwell, and in Acts 19:24, small silver models of temples of the goddess Artemis are made.
2. More specifically, it is the most secret and holy place of the temple, the inner sanctuary that only the priest could approach. Luke 1:21 shows Zechariah who "remained a long time in the temple" while performing his priestly service at the heart of the building.
3. When speaking of Jerusalem, the word refers to the sacred building itself—the structure where the altar and sacred vessels are located—distinct from the entire courtyard with its outer areas. Jesus announces that "this temple will be destroyed" and that He will rebuild it in three days (Matthew 27:40; John 2:19-20), which provokes the anger of the authorities.
4. Paul and Peter apply the word to the Christians themselves: "you are the temple of the living God" (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16). The people of God become His house, His dwelling. It is a breathtaking image: each believer, each church community has become what the stone building once was.
5. John 2:21 reveals that Jesus was speaking of His own body as the temple: "He was speaking of the temple of His body." After His resurrection, His body becomes the new center of God's presence, replacing the material temple.
G3485.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to dwell." In Hebrew, the temple is called "heikhal," a term that the Greek Bible rightly renders as "naos." This is because the temple is primarily the place where God dwells, where He establishes His presence among men. The preposition "in" or "within" often accompanies this word to say "in the temple," emphasizing the idea of a defined, sacred space where one enters to encounter the divine.
G3485.emploi: The word appears about forty times in the New Testament. In the Gospels and Acts, it almost always refers to the temple of Jerusalem or its sacred parts: it speaks of oaths by the temple (Matthew 23:16-17), its destruction announced by Jesus (Matthew 27:40; Mark 14:58; John 2:19), and the veil that is torn at His death (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38). In Paul's epistles, the word changes meaning: it becomes an image of the Church and believers. In Revelation, it describes the heavenly temple of the visions, for example, during the final vision where God will dwell with men and where "there will be no temple" made of material (Revelation 21:22) because God and the Lamb will be the temple.
G3485.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God desires to dwell among His people. The transition from the stone temple to the living temple (the Christians) shows that God's presence no longer depends on a building, but on the presence of the Holy Spirit in the heart and community. Knowing that we are the temple of God is a source of reverence: it calls us to honor God by taking care of our bodies and our fraternal relationships. Finally, the revelation that the body of Christ has become the temple invites us to understand that it is now in Him and through Him that we access God.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G3486.detail: Nahum is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy that Luke gives of Jesus tracing back to Adam. He appears as the son of Mattathias and the father of Esli, situated about sixteen generations before Jesus (Luke 3:25). This name appears in the ancestral line of Christ according to the Gospel of Luke.
G3486.origine: The name Nahum comes from the Hebrew נַחוּם (Nahum), which means "comfort" or "consoler." It is a theophoric name carrying the idea of divine consolation. It can be related to the Hebrew verb נִחַם (niham), "to comfort." The prophet Nahum, author of the book that bears his name in the Old Testament, shares the same root and meaning, although he is a different person living several centuries before the time of Jesus.
G3486.emploi: Nahum appears only once in the Scriptures, in Luke 3:25, where Luke mentions him in his genealogy of Jesus. Unlike the prophet Nahum of the Old Testament, this Nahum is merely a link in the genealogical chain: nothing else is known about his life. Luke includes his name to establish the continuity of David's lineage to Jesus, thus demonstrating the legitimate origins of the Messiah.

sens: Tropical aromatic plant from which a precious perfume is derived
Liquid perfume obtained from this plant, used for anointing or embalming
G3487.detail:
1. Nard is a plant native to India (its name comes from Sanskrit), which produces a highly sought fragrance in antiquity. It was notably used to prepare luxury ointments. The Bible mentions it in the Song of Solomon as a precious scent (Song of Solomon 4:13-14).

2. By extension, the word refers to the perfume itself, this liquid ointment of great value. This meaning predominates in the Gospel accounts: a woman in Bethany pours "pure nard of great price" on Jesus from an alabaster jar (Mark 14:3), and Mary anoints Jesus' feet with a pound of pure nard, filling the house with its fragrance (John 12:3). This act expresses honor and love towards Jesus through the gift of the most precious possession.
G3487.origine: The word nard, in Greek νάρδος (nardos), comes from the Sanskrit narda. It originally refers to the plant Nardostachys nardus jatamansi, cultivated in India and the Himalayas. The Hebrew word נֵרְדְּ (nerd) has the same etymology. In Greek, this word has settled to designate both the plant and, by common metonymy, the precious perfume extracted from it. It is a borrowing from the vocabulary of Eastern trade, reflecting the exchanges between the Mediterranean world and India.
G3487.emploi: The word nard appears only twice in the New Testament, both times by the evangelists to designate the luxury perfume used in homage to Jesus. In Mark 14:3, a woman pours pure nard on Jesus' head while he is at the table in the house of Simon the leper, an act that provokes the indignation of the disciples due to its exorbitant cost. In John 12:3, it is Mary of Bethany who anoints Jesus' feet with pure nard, an act of remarkable tenderness. In both cases, nard symbolizes respect, love, and mourning towards Jesus, and its high price underscores the extraordinary nature of the gift. The Old Testament mentions nard among the perfumes of the king in the Song of Solomon.
G3487.portee: These two accounts show how authentic faith expresses itself through sincere giving, without calculation. The price of nard — a year's wages — reminds us that giving to Jesus what we have of most precious is never wasteful: it is to recognize his dignity and his love for us. These women become models of devotion, and their actions invite us to consider what we are willing to sacrifice for the Lord.

sens: Christian mentioned in Rome
G3488.detail: This refers to a Christian from the household of Narcissus in Rome, whose faithful members Paul greets in his letter to this church. The name was common among slaves and imperial affiliates of the time, suggesting that Narcissus may have been a notable Roman who embraced the faith. Paul mentions him only here, with no further details about his life or role.
G3488.origine: The Greek name Νάρκισσος (Narkissos) comes from the verb ναρκάω (narkáô), which means to numb, as the plant of the same name had narcotic properties. In Greek mythology, Narcissus is a young man cursed to love himself, but the biblical character has no connection to this legend: it is simply a name borne by a Roman Christian.
G3488.emploi: Narcissus is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:11. Paul sends greetings to those of his household — that is, his slaves, clients, or dependents — who believed in Jesus. The context suggests that he was an influential person in Rome, as an entire household was associated with him, and some of its members had joined the Church. This is an example of the presence of nascent Christianity even within the domestic circles of the Roman elite.

sens: To be shipwrecked, to perish at sea with one's ship
To lose, abandon, or destroy something precious, especially faith
G3489.detail:
1. To make shipwreck literally means to suffer the disaster of a ship sinking or running aground at sea. Paul uses it in the literal sense when recounting his sufferings: "three times I was shipwrecked, I spent a day and a night in the deep" (2 Corinthians 11:25). It is the brutal experience of a sailor at the mercy of the waves.
2. The word is used figuratively to describe moral or spiritual destruction: losing faith, capsizing one's conscience, abandoning what should save us. In 1 Timothy 1:19, Paul speaks of those "who have made shipwreck concerning the faith" — their trust in God has collapsed like a sinking ship. The image is striking: one loses footing, one can no longer cling to anything.
G3489.origine: The Greek word comes from "naos" (ship) and a verb meaning "to break, to shatter": to make shipwreck literally means to break a ship. It is a natural image for Greeks and Romans, a seafaring people. Applied to faith or conscience, the image of shipwreck expresses complete collapse, total loss — like a sailor sinking, one disappears.
G3489.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in very different contexts. In 2 Corinthians 11:25, Paul testifies to the shipwreck he actually experienced during his missionary journeys — it is a fact of his apostolic biography. In 1 Timothy 1:19, the same word describes the spiritual disaster of those who abandon their faith: the shipwreck becomes a metaphor for inner ruin. Paul thus uses the same word to depict a real physical misfortune and a catastrophe of the soul.
G3489.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith resembles a journey at sea: there are storms, perils, moments when one risks sinking. But making shipwreck is never fatal if one clings to God. For Paul, having survived real shipwrecks shows that God was protecting him; for the reader, it is a call to hold firm to faith and conscience, the two anchors that prevent us from making spiritual shipwreck.

sens: owner and commander of a merchant ship
one who has authority over the ship and its crew
G3490.detail:
1. The master of the ship is the owner or shipowner who commands a merchant vessel. This is a person of high social status, responsible for the cargo and navigation. In Acts 27:11, it is he whom the centurion listens to rather than the apostle Paul, which shows his recognized authority.
2. Broadly speaking, he is the one who directs the ship and makes important decisions during the voyage: which route to take, when to depart, how to face storms. The master was credited with experience and skill that the other passengers respected.
G3490.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: ναῦς (ship) and κλῆρος (part, portion, which comes from a verb meaning to draw lots or assign). The master was literally the one who had the 'part' of the ship, meaning its possession and command. This term shows how the Greeks and Romans designated the chief responsible for a merchant ship.
G3490.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:11, in the account of Paul's shipwreck. During the storm in the Mediterranean, the centurion guarding the prisoners must choose between following the advice of the pilot and the master of the ship, or listening to the warning that Paul, inspired by the Spirit, addresses to them. The context shows that the master, along with the pilot, represented maritime authority and the world's trust in its own competencies.
G3490.portee: This account invites reflection on whom we listen to and in whom we place our trust. The master and the pilot, despite their earthly experience, were unaware of what God had revealed to Paul. This reminds us that human wisdom, even legitimate in its field, can be mistaken in the face of what only God knows.

sens: Large boat designed for maritime navigation
Vessel capable of crossing seas and oceans
G3491.detail:
1. The ship is a boat designed to navigate the sea, large and sturdy enough to face waves and transport passengers or goods over long distances. It is the word used to describe the vessel that runs aground during Paul's shipwreck on the way to Rome: 'they ran aground on a certain island' (Acts 27:41).
2. The ship is a complete maritime vessel, with its various parts such as the bow and stern mentioned in the account of the shipwreck, which made it an imposing craft capable of facing the storms and dangers of the Mediterranean Sea.
G3491.origine: The Greek word ναῦς (naus) comes from an Indo-European root meaning boat. In Hebrew, there are similar terms like אֲנִיָּה (ania) or עָנִי (ani) also used to refer to ships. This word belongs to the ancient maritime vocabulary and was well known to the Greeks, a seafaring people. It is a classical term in ancient Greek, distinct from the word πλοῖον (ploïon) which also means boat but was more common in the New Testament.
G3491.emploi: The word ναῦς appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:41, during the account of the shipwreck of the vessel carrying Paul. This unique usage shows that Luke, the author of Acts, chose this precise and more solemn term to describe this particular maritime vessel, probably because it was a large transport ship. The term ναῦς was more classical and literary, while πλοῖον (ploïon) was the everyday term in Greek for boats.
G3491.portee: This account of the shipwreck shows God's faithfulness to Paul in the midst of extreme danger: while the ship is breaking apart and everything seems lost, the Church learns that God protects His servant and saves all the passengers. This story teaches the reader that trust in God remains valid even in the face of storms and circumstances that seem desperate.

sens: Person who works on a ship, responsible for its maneuvering and operation
Broadly, all those who live and work at sea
G3492.detail:
1. A sailor is a crew member who operates the boat — he raises the sails, handles the ropes, monitors navigation. In Acts 27, during Paul's shipwreck, it is the sailors who attempt to escape the ship by secretly lowering the lifeboat (Acts 27:30), and they are also the ones who, at night, suspect they are nearing land (Acts 27:27).
2. More broadly, the word designates all seafaring people — mariners, navigators, all those whose profession depends on the ocean. In Revelation 18:17, in the vision of the fall of Babylon, all the sailors flee far away, terrified, because the city that enriched them through maritime trade is destroyed.
G3492.origine: The word comes from the Greek ναῦς (naus), which means 'boat' or 'ship'. The sailor is therefore literally 'the man of the boat'. It is a simple and direct word, without particular nuance: it primarily designates the worker of the sea, the one who lives on or with the ship.
G3492.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts of travel or maritime disaster. In Acts 27, it places Paul at sea during his transfer to Rome: the sailors are living characters, with their fears and strategies to survive the shipwreck. In Revelation 18, the word serves to paint the universal terror caused by the destruction of Babylon, the great trading city: the sailors, who depended on its commerce, gaze from afar at the smoke of its burning. In all cases, the sailor is presented as an ordinary man, caught up in events that surpass him.
G3492.portee: These passages remind us that God governs even the storms and the seas — Paul, a prisoner on a perilous ship, remains under divine protection, while the sailors, despite their experience, cannot save the ship (Acts 27). The image of the sailors fleeing Babylon also shows that God's judgment reaches all men, rich or humble, powerful or simple workers.

sens: ancestor of Abraham in the genealogy of Jesus
G3493.detail: Nahor is a biblical character mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke. He is presented as the father of Terah, who is himself the father of Abraham (Luke 3:34). He appears in the lineage that traces back from Jesus to Adam, emphasizing that Jesus is part of the history of the people of Israel and is the heir of the promises made to the patriarchs.
G3493.origine: The name Nahor comes from the Hebrew נָחוֹר (Nahor), which already appears in the Old Testament in Genesis 11:22-26 as one of the direct ancestors of Abraham. He is an ancient figure in the pre-flood genealogy of the Hebrew people, recorded in the lineage of Shem, son of Noah.
G3493.emploi: Nahor appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:34, where the apostle Luke establishes the complete genealogy of Jesus tracing back to Adam. This genealogical passage occurs just after the baptism of Jesus and serves to affirm that Jesus, although the Son of God, is also part of the historical continuity of Abraham's people and inherits the promises made to him.
G3493.portee: This genealogical passage reminds the reader that Jesus did not come outside of the history of Israel's salvation, but is its fulfillment. By placing Jesus in an unbroken chain that traces back to the distant ancestors of Abraham, Luke shows that the Incarnation responds to ancient promises and is rooted in God's faithfulness to His people.

sens: A boy or young man, in the age of adolescence or early adulthood
A young man in contrast to older individuals
G3494.detail:
1. The word designates an adolescent or young adult, typically a boy or young man capable of acting and moving. It is Saul (who will become the Apostle Paul) who guards the clothes during the martyrdom of Stephen in Acts 7:58, or Eutychus, the young man who falls asleep at the window and falls from the third story in Acts 20:9 — the latter example shows the vulnerability and inattention of youth.
2. The word sometimes emphasizes age as a distinctive trait: in Acts 23:17, Paul calls for "a young man" to carry a message to the tribune, which underscores his youth and likely his liveliness for such a task.
G3494.origine: The word comes from the Greek νέος (néos), which means "new" or "young." It is a diminutive or a form emphasizing youth. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew נַעַר (na'ar), which designates a young boy or servant, and בָּחוּר (bachur), a young man of fighting or working age.
G3494.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Acts. It describes particular individuals: first the young Saul who guards the clothes at Stephen's martyrdom, then Eutychus whom Paul must revive after his fall, and finally an anonymous messenger whom Paul charges with a mission to the tribune. In each case, the age of the character is relevant to the narrative — either to show that a renowned young man (Saul) approved of Stephen's death, or to highlight the tragedy and miracle of a resurrection, or to suggest the ability of the young to accomplish a swift task.
G3494.portee: This word reminds us that youth, in Scripture, carries both a promise and a vulnerability. Saul began his life in error, guarding the cloaks of Stephen's executioners, but became the Apostle Paul: youth is never static. The sleeping Eutychus shows how a young person can be fragile and mortal, but also how God's power raises him up. Thus, the term invites us to see young people not as negligible, but as actors whose lives God can transform.

sens: Boy or adolescent in the process of growing up, not yet an adult
Young people or young men, in their prime
Servant or assistant to an important person
Celestial being or angelic messenger appearing in the form of a young man
G3495.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a child or adolescent who is growing, distinct from a small child. In Matthew 19:20 and 19:22, the young man who questions Jesus about eternal life is mature enough to have accumulated wealth and make his own decisions, yet still young.
2. The term also designates young people of a generation, particularly those endowed with physical and mental strength. In Acts 2:17, the prophecy announces that young people will have visions: it is the energy and receptivity of youth.
3. It can name a servant or personal assistant, as in Acts 5:10 where the young man who buries Sapphira is part of the apostolic group's service.
4. Three times, the word designates a celestial being: the young man dressed in white who guards the tomb in Mark 16:5 is likely an angel; the young man fleeing naked during Jesus' arrest in Mark 14:51 remains enigmatic regarding his identity.
G3495.origine: The word νεανίσκος (neaniskos) is the diminutive of the name νεανίας (neanias), formed from the root νέος (neos) which means "new" or "young." This root expresses the idea of what begins, of what is not yet aged. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the Greek of the Septuagint translates this word by נַעַר (na'ar), which designates a boy or young servant, and by בָּחוּר (bachur), which means a vigorous young man.
G3495.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It often describes young people in relation to an event or an important person: the rich young man questioning Jesus (Matthew), a young man following Jesus at Gethsemane (Mark 14:51), the one who proclaims the resurrection at the tomb (Mark 16:5). In Acts, the term applies to young converts and disciples, notably the "young men" who have visions in Acts 2:17. The word can also designate an official or messenger, as in Acts 23:18 where a young man reports to the Roman police. Its use in 1 John 2:13-14 contrasts the "young men" with the "fathers" and "children," marking the generations of faith.
G3495.portee: This word reminds us that youth, far from being foreign to God's work, is an important actor: young people receive visions, the rich young man is called to a radical decision before Jesus. It invites the reader to recognize the vitality and spiritual responsibility of the young, without underestimating them. It is an implicit call: youth is not a time of passive waiting, but of engaging choices before God.

sens: Syrian military officer, general or chief of the army of the king of Syria
Man afflicted with leprosy who was healed by the prophet Elisha
G3497.detail: 1. Naaman was an important figure: a high-ranking officer, possibly a general, in the service of the king of Syria. He was a man of power and prestige in the neighboring kingdom of Israel. 2. He suffered from leprosy, a serious disease that rendered the sick impure according to the law of Israel. Despite his high social status and wealth, this disease afflicted him without the Syrian doctors being able to heal him. 3. Elisha miraculously healed him by commanding him to dip seven times in the Jordan. This healing became a sign of God's power and grace towards foreigners. In Luke 4:27, Jesus mentions him to show that God has historically extended His holy hand beyond Israel, even to Israel's enemies, when they turned to Him in faith.
G3497.origine: The Hebrew name נַעֲמָן (Na'aman) means "pleasant" or "sweet." It is a personal name borne by this famous Syrian commander who is detailed in the account of the second book of Kings. The Greek simply reproduces the Hebrew name as it is, as it is a well-known historical figure.
G3497.emploi: Naaman appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:27, where Jesus cites him as an example. Jesus mentions him during His discourse in Nazareth to illustrate how God performed miracles in favor of foreigners, including Israel's enemies, rather than in favor of the Israelites themselves. This example shows that divine grace is not limited to national or religious boundaries, but is offered to anyone who believes. The New Testament thus takes up this account from the Old Testament to teach a lesson about the universality of God's mercy.
G3497.portee: The example of Naaman reminds the Christian reader that God does not regard social status, nationality, or even the hostility of a people: He grants His healing and grace to those who come to Him with humility and trust. It is an encouragement for every believer, regardless of their background, to believe that God can touch and transform them.

sens: Lifeless, having ceased to live
Raised from the dead
Spiritually dead, separated from God
Devoid of effectiveness or power
G3498.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: a person or body deprived of life. In Luke 7:22, Jesus says that the "dead are raised" among the signs of the Messiah; in Acts 5:10, Sapphira falls "dead" after God's judgment.
2. Raised or brought back to life. The word refers to one who comes out of the tomb, from the power of death. In Romans 4:24, it is "he who was raised from the dead Jesus our Lord" — Jesus himself was raised "from the dead," passing from death to eternal life.
3. Spiritually lifeless, cut off from God. In Romans 6:11, the believer is urged to consider themselves as "dead to sin": as someone who no longer obeys the power of sin. In John 5:25, "the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God" refers to those who are spiritually dead, prisoners of sin and judgment.
4. Ineffective, without power to act. In James 2:26, "faith without works is dead": it has no power, it produces nothing. In Hebrews 9:14, the "dead works" are religious acts that do not purify the conscience — empty, barren acts.
G3498.origine: The Greek word νεκρός comes from an ancient Indo-European root and primarily denotes the absence of life. It generally translates the Hebrew מֵת (mèt, dead) in the Greek Old Testament. The word family includes νεκρόω (to make dead, kill), ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν (resurrection of the dead), and other forms. It is a fundamental term in biblical thought regarding physical and spiritual death.
G3498.emploi: The word appears more than 120 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. It is first used in the literal sense: corpses, the deceased (Matthew 8:22: "let the dead bury their own dead"). It also refers to those who are resurrected: Jesus "raised from the dead" is the heart of the Gospel (Romans 4:24, Acts 3:15). Paul frequently uses it in a figurative sense to speak of the spiritual death of sin and the new life in Christ: being "dead to sin" and "alive to God" (Romans 6:11, 6:13). It also qualifies what has become inoperative: a "dead" faith without works (James 2:26), "dead works" that do not save (Hebrews 9:14).
G3498.portee: This word is at the heart of the Christian faith: it reminds us that only God has power over death and life, and that Jesus, by rising "from the dead," has conquered death and offers all believers resurrection. It also invites the Christian to see their spiritual death to sin as real and liberating: to consider oneself as dead to sin is to embrace the liberating power of Christ. Finally, it warns that faith without works is barren: true faith produces a new life.

sens: To cause to die, take away life
To be inert, powerless, helpless (of a person or an organ)
To eliminate, annihilate (in a figurative sense)
G3499.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the verb means to cause to die or kill. This is the literal meaning of the root, even if it does not explicitly appear in the provided biblical usages.

2. In a figurative and hyperbolic sense, it describes powerlessness or inertia: Abraham at nearly a hundred years had a body "worn out," that is, become like dead, incapable of giving life naturally (Romans 4:19; Hebrews 11:12). The image is that of a vital force extinguished.

3. In a moral and spiritual sense, Paul urges Christians to "put to death" (annihilate, eliminate) the carnal desires — impurity, covetousness — that dwell in their members (Colossians 3:5). It is a call to voluntarily stifle these sinful tendencies, as one would kill a rebellion.
G3499.origine: The verb comes from the adjective νεκρός (nekros, "dead"), which conveys the idea of being inert, lifeless. The root evokes physical death, but it also applies to what is devoid of power or function. In Greek, νεκρόω is constructed with an object (what is made dead) and describes an action that deprives of life, vigor, or effectiveness.
G3499.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the provided New Testament, always in a figurative sense. In Romans 4:19 and Hebrews 11:12, it describes Abraham's body as worn out and powerless despite his advanced age — a partial death that does not prevent the miracle of the promise. In Colossians 3:5, Paul uses it morally: believers must "put to death" their members subjected to carnal sins, that is, actively renounce impure desires. The word moves from the physical domain to the voluntary and ethical domain: from inevitable death to the death one inflicts upon oneself to live in Christ.
G3499.portee: This verb invites the Christian to a struggle: to recognize that certain desires must be "killed" for the Spirit to live in them. It is also a reminder that God's power often acts in human weakness and helplessness — as with Abraham — revealing that only faith and divine promise can resurrect what is dead. The word articulates two dimensions of the Christian life: active renunciation and trust in a power that surpasses our strength.
